bank.why: Carbamates = the -stigmines (neostigmine, pyridostigmine, physostigmine). Edrophonium is an alcohol; parathion and malathion are organophosphates.

dw.Edrophonium: Edrophonium is a short-acting alcohol-type inhibitor.

bank.q: A child who swallowed eye drops containing atropine is delirious, hot and dry. Which AChE inhibitor reaches the brain and reverses it?
bank.why: Physostigmine is a tertiary amine that enters the CNS; it treats atropine (anticholinergic) overdose.

dw.Neostigmine: Neostigmine does not cross into the brain.
dw.Pyridostigmine: Pyridostigmine does not cross into the brain.
dw.Edrophonium: Edrophonium does not cross into the brain.

bank.q: Which is an irreversible AChE inhibitor used as a pesticide?
bank.why: Organophosphates (-thion: parathion, malathion) inhibit AChE irreversibly. -THION = THE ONE you can't undo.

dw.Edrophonium: Edrophonium is a short-acting reversible inhibitor.
dw.Donepezil: Donepezil is a reversible inhibitor for Alzheimer disease.

bank.q: Which of these was a war nerve gas (WWII)?
bank.why: Tabun, sarin and soman are nerve gases; parathion and malathion are pesticides. All are organophosphates.
bank.hint: The other three are two pesticides and a short-acting test drug.

bank.q: What do nerve agents such as sarin directly target?
bank.why: Organophosphate nerve agents bind AChE irreversibly, so ACh builds up. Past quiz item.

dw.Nicotinic receptors: Nicotinic receptors are not the target of sarin.
dw.Muscarinic receptors: Muscarinic receptors are not the direct target.
dw.Choline acetyltransferase: ChAT makes ACh; sarin does not block it.

bank.q: Which drug is NOT used for Alzheimer disease?
bank.why: Alzheimer drugs: donepezil, galantamine, rivastigmine ("Si Don Pepe, may dementia. Pa Gala Gala sa Riva"). The past quiz version had physostigmine as the answer.

dw.Donepezil: Donepezil is used for Alzheimer disease.
dw.Rivastigmine: Rivastigmine is used for Alzheimer disease.
dw.Galantamine: Galantamine is used for Alzheimer disease.

bank.q: Lolo Ben has slowly worsening memory loss diagnosed as Alzheimer disease. Which drug is used?
bank.why: Donepezil, galantamine and rivastigmine are AChE inhibitors for Alzheimer (cholinergic neurons are deficient).

dw.Edrophonium: Edrophonium is a diagnostic, short-acting drug.
dw.Pyridostigmine: Pyridostigmine does not enter the brain.

bank.q: Why are AChE inhibitors used in Alzheimer dementia?
bank.a: Cholinergic neurons are deficient in Alzheimer disease
d: They increase dopamine in the brain
bank.why: Slides: cholinergic neurons are deficient, so making ACh last longer helps.

dw.They block NMDA receptors: Blocking NMDA receptors is memantine's action.

bank.q: Which lists the AChE inhibitors from SHORTEST to LONGEST acting?
bank.why: Short: edrophonium; intermediate: carbamates (-stigmines); very long: organophosphates (-thion).

dw.Edrophonium → parathion → neostigmine: Parathion, an irreversible inhibitor, lasts longest.

bank.q: Physostigmine enters the CNS, which is why it is used for atropine overdose.
bank.why: Physostigmine is a tertiary amine and crosses into the brain; neostigmine does not.

bank.q: Organophosphates such as parathion are reversible AChE inhibitors.
bank.why: Organophosphates inhibit AChE irreversibly.

bank.q: The three groups of cholinergic antagonists are...
bank.why: Antimuscarinic (atropine…), antinicotinic (ganglion and NMJ blockers) and cholinesterase regenerators (oximes like pralidoxime).

dw.Direct, indirect and mixed: Direct, indirect and mixed describe agonists.
dw.Carbamates, organophosphates and alcohol: Carbamates, organophosphates and alcohols are cholinesterase inhibitors.
dw.α, β and mixed blockers: α, β and mixed blockers are adrenergic antagonists.

bank.q: Pralidoxime (2-PAM) belongs to which group?
bank.why: Oximes regenerate AChE after organophosphate poisoning.

bank.q: A farmer poisoned with organophosphate pesticide is drooling, wheezing, with pinpoint pupils. Which drug is the first choice?
bank.why: Atropine blocks the muscarinic effects of the excess ACh: first choice for organophosphate poisoning (with pralidoxime). The other three add cholinergic effect.

dw.Physostigmine: Physostigmine is a cholinesterase inhibitor and would worsen the poisoning.
dw.Neostigmine: Neostigmine is a cholinesterase inhibitor and would worsen the poisoning.
dw.Bethanechol: Bethanechol is a muscarinic agonist and would add to the excess.

bank.q: A patient's heart rate is 38/min and he feels faint. Which drug raises the heart rate by blocking vagal (muscarinic) tone?
bank.why: Atropine is used for symptomatic bradycardia; propranolol, neostigmine and pilocarpine would slow the heart more.

dw.Propranolol: Propranolol is a β-blocker and would slow the heart further.
dw.Neostigmine: Neostigmine raises ACh and slows the heart.
dw.Pilocarpine: Pilocarpine is a muscarinic agonist and would slow the heart.

bank.q: During general anesthesia, atropine is given to...
bank.a: Prevent bradycardia and reduce saliva and airway secretions
d: Relax skeletal muscle so the trachea can be intubated
Induce sleep and deepen the anesthetic
Prevent malignant hyperthermia from volatile agents
bank.why: Slides: with anesthesia for bradycardia, hypersalivation and airway secretions.

dw.Relax skeletal muscle so the trachea can: Skeletal muscle relaxation is the job of neuromuscular blockers.
dw.Prevent malignant hyperthermia from vola: Dantrolene, not atropine, treats malignant hyperthermia.

bank.term: Pupil dilation for an eye exam
bank.q: An ophthalmologist needs to dilate a patient's pupils for a retinal exam. Which eye drop?
bank.why: Tropicamide (like atropine, homatropine, cyclopentolate) is an antimuscarinic mydriatic. Pilocarpine constricts the pupil; tiotropium is inhaled.

dw.Timolol: Timolol lowers eye pressure in glaucoma.

bank.q: Christopher has COPD. Which inhaled drug blocks bronchial muscarinic receptors and has the longest half-life?
bank.why: -tropium drugs (ipratropium, tiotropium) plus umeclidinium and glycopyrronium are inhaled for asthma and COPD; tiotropium lasts longest.

dw.Scopolamine: Scopolamine is used for motion sickness.
dw.Dicyclomine: Dicyclomine is used for GI spasm.

bank.q: Which inhaled antimuscarinic has the longest half-life?
bank.why: Slides: tiotropium has the longest half-life.

dw.Glycopyrronium: Glycopyrronium is shorter acting than tiotropium.
dw.Umeclidinium: Umeclidinium is shorter acting than tiotropium.

bank.q: Reine gets seasick on every boat trip. Which antimuscarinic prevents motion sickness?
bank.why: Scopolamine (a stereoisomer of atropine) crosses the blood-brain barrier better → motion sickness. Scop = sea.

dw.Atropine: Atropine does not cross into the brain as well as scopolamine.
dw.Oxybutynin: Oxybutynin is used for overactive bladder.
dw.Pirenzepine: Pirenzepine is used for peptic ulcer disease.

bank.q: Why is scopolamine preferred over atropine for motion sickness?
bank.a: It crosses the blood-brain barrier better
d: It acts only on M2 receptors
bank.why: Scopolamine reaches the CNS better than atropine.

dw.It acts only on M2 receptors: It is not limited to M2 receptors.
dw.It has no side effects: It has the usual antimuscarinic side effects.
dw.It is a nicotinic blocker: It blocks muscarinic, not nicotinic, receptors.

bank.q: Lola Ising leaks urine whenever she feels a sudden urge to void. Which drug relaxes the bladder?
bank.why: Oxybutynin (M3 blocker) for urge incontinence. Bethanechol does the opposite (retention); tamsulosin is for BPH; dicyclomine is the M3 blocker for diarrhea.

dw.Bethanechol: Bethanechol is a muscarinic agonist and would make leakage worse.
dw.Tamsulosin: Tamsulosin relaxes the prostate and bladder neck, not the detrusor.
dw.Dicyclomine: Dicyclomine is used for GI spasm.

bank.q: Which M3 blocker is used for diarrhea?
bank.why: Dicyclomine (dicycloverine) for diarrhea; oxybutynin for the bladder; pirenzepine for ulcers.

dw.Pirenzepine: Pirenzepine is an M1 blocker for ulcers.

bank.q: Which M1-selective blocker lowers gastric acid in peptic ulcer disease?
bank.why: Pirenzepine and telenzepine (M1) reduce acid secretion → peptic ulcer disease.

dw.Dicyclomine: Dicyclomine is M3 for GI spasm.

bank.q: Which drug blocks Nn receptors in the autonomic ganglia and was once used for hypertension?
bank.why: Hexamethonium is the ganglionic (Nn) blocker, now obsolete.

dw.Pancuronium: Pancuronium blocks Nm at the neuromuscular junction.
dw.Succinylcholine: Succinylcholine is a depolarizing neuromuscular blocker.

bank.q: Before surgery, an anesthesiologist gives a drug that blocks Nm receptors to relax skeletal muscle. Which drug did the anesthesiologist give?
bank.why: Curares (tubocurarine, pancuronium, atracurium, vecuronium) block Nm at the NMJ.

dw.Hexamethonium: Hexamethonium blocks Nn receptors in the ganglia.
dw.Neostigmine: Neostigmine increases ACh, which would not relax muscle.

bank.q: Which drug is NOT a neuromuscular (curare-like) blocker?
bank.why: Hexamethonium blocks ganglia (Nn), not the NMJ (Nm).

bank.q: Scopolamine is related to atropine as its...
bank.why: Slides: scopolamine is a stereoisomer of atropine.

dw.Metabolite: Scopolamine is not a metabolite of atropine.
dw.Prodrug: It is not an inactive precursor, so not a prodrug.
dw.Antagonist: It has the same antimuscarinic action; it does not oppose atropine.

bank.q: Atropine blocks all muscarinic receptors.
bank.why: Atropine is the nonselective prototype muscarinic blocker.

bank.q: Which is NOT a catecholamine?
bank.why: The catecholamines are norepinephrine, epinephrine and dopamine.

bank.q: What is the order of catecholamine synthesis?
bank.why: Tyrosine hydroxylase → AAAD → dopamine β-hydroxylase → PNMT.

bank.q: What is the rate-limiting enzyme of catecholamine synthesis?
bank.why: Tyrosine hydroxylase (tyrosine → L-DOPA) is rate-limiting; metyrosine inhibits it.

dw.PNMT: PNMT comes last, in the adrenal medulla.

bank.q: Which enzyme converts norepinephrine to epinephrine in the adrenal medulla?
bank.why: PNMT (phenylethanolamine N-methyltransferase) adds the methyl that makes epinephrine.

dw.Dopamine β-hydroxylase: Dopamine β-hydroxylase makes norepinephrine from dopamine.

bank.q: Which drug inhibits tyrosine hydroxylase?
bank.why: Met Reserve Guards at Coco's: metyrosine (synthesis), reserpine (storage), guanethidine (release), cocaine/TCA (reuptake).

bank.q: Which drug blocks VMAT, so catecholamines can't be stored in vesicles?
bank.why: Reserpine blocks VMAT. Vesamicol is the cholinergic look-alike (blocks VAT for ACh).

bank.q: Which drug blocks the release of norepinephrine?
bank.why: Guanethidine blocks release; amphetamine and tyramine cause release; cocaine blocks reuptake.

bank.q: Which drug CAUSES the release of norepinephrine?
bank.why: Release is activated by amphetamines, ephedrine and tyramine.

bank.q: Steve's blood test shows cocaine. How does cocaine increase norepinephrine in the synapse?
bank.a: It blocks NE reuptake through NET
bank.why: Cocaine and tricyclic antidepressants block the reuptake transporters (NET, DAT), so NE stays in the synapse. (A midterm case started with "Steve has cocaine in his blood".)

dw.It stimulates tyrosine hydroxylase: Cocaine does not act on tyrosine hydroxylase.

bank.q: Which drug class blocks NE reuptake like cocaine?
bank.why: Termination by reuptake (NET) is blocked by cocaine and TCAs.

dw.MAO inhibitors: MAO inhibitors block metabolism, not reuptake.

bank.q: Tyramine, found in aged cheese and cured meats, acts by...
bank.why: Tyramine is an NE releaser (a migraine trigger).

dw.Blocking α1 receptors: Tyramine releases NE; it does not block α1.

bank.q: Which food is rich in tyramine?
bank.why: Aged foods: cheese, cured meats, beer, soy sauce, overripe fruit.

bank.q: Vesamicol is to ACh storage as ___ is to catecholamine storage.
bank.why: Side by side: storage = vesamicol (ACh) vs reserpine (NE).

bank.q: Botulinum toxin is to ACh release as ___ is to NE release.
bank.why: Release: botulinum (ACh) vs guanethidine (NE).

bank.q: Which receptor increases heart rate and contractility?
bank.why: β1 = one heart; β2 = two lungs; α1 = squeeze (vasoconstriction); α2 = slow down (presynaptic brake).

bank.q: Which receptor causes bronchodilation?
bank.why: β2 = two lungs.

bank.q: Which receptor causes vasoconstriction and sphincter contraction?
bank.why: α1 = contraction (squeeze).

bank.q: Which receptor acts as a presynaptic brake on norepinephrine release?
bank.why: α2 = relaxation and the presynaptic brake; that's why α2 agonists (clonidine, methyldopa) lower BP.

bank.q: A patient in septic shock has a BP of 70/40 despite fluids. Which drug is first line?
bank.why: Norepinephrine (α1 > β1) raises peripheral resistance: first line in septic shock.

dw.Epinephrine: Epinephrine is not first line in septic shock.
dw.Isoproterenol: Isoproterenol is a nonselective β agonist.

bank.q: Minutes after a bee sting, a boy has hives, wheezing and a falling BP. Which drug should he be given first?
bank.why: Epinephrine (β1 = β2 > α) opens the airways (β2), supports the heart (β1) and vessels (α): drug of choice in anaphylaxis (EpiPen).

dw.Norepinephrine: Norepinephrine is not the drug for anaphylaxis.
dw.Phenylephrine: Phenylephrine is an α1 agonist only.

bank.q: Epinephrine's receptor profile is...
bank.why: Epi = "every"one; NE = "no" β2 (α1 > β1 >>> β2).

bank.q: Norepinephrine's receptor profile is...
bank.why: Norepinephrine has little β2 effect ("no β2").

bank.q: At LOW doses, dopamine mainly stimulates...
bank.why: Dopamine climbs D → β → α as the dose rises.

dw.β1 receptors (tachycardia): β1 is stimulated at medium doses.
dw.α1 receptors (vasoconstriction): α1 is stimulated at high doses.
dw.β2 receptors (bronchodilation): β2 is not the main low-dose effect.

bank.q: At HIGH doses, dopamine mainly stimulates...
bank.why: Low D1, middle β1, high α1.

dw.D1 receptors (renal vasodilation): D1 renal vasodilation is the low-dose effect.
dw.β2 receptors (bronchodilation): β2 is not the main high-dose effect.
dw.M2 receptors (slower heart rate): M2 is a muscarinic receptor; dopamine does not act there.

bank.q: Dopamine is first line in septic shock when there is also...
bank.why: Slides: dopamine, first line in septic shock with renal shutdown (its D1 effect dilates renal vessels).

dw.Asthma: Asthma needs a β2 agonist, not dopamine.
dw.Bradycardia only: Bradycardia alone is not the reason.

bank.q: Janah has a stuffy nose from a cold. Which nasal spray shrinks the nasal vessels?
bank.why: α1 agonists (phenylephrine, pseudoephedrine, oxymetazoline, tetrahydrozoline) are decongestants.

dw.Clonidine: Clonidine is an α2 agonist for hypertension.

bank.q: Which drug is an α1 agonist used as a decongestant?
bank.why: α1 agonists: phenylephrine, pseudoephedrine, oxymetazoline, tetrahydrozoline.

dw.Isoproterenol: Isoproterenol is a nonselective β agonist.

bank.q: Which α2 agonist is used for hypertension and off-label for ADHD and Tourette syndrome?
bank.why: Clonidine: α2 → hypertension; off-label ADHD and Tourette. Methyldopa is the α2 agonist for pregnancy.

dw.Methyldopa: Methyldopa is an α2 agonist, used in pregnancy.

bank.q: A pregnant woman at 32 weeks has preeclampsia. Which α2 agonist is used for her blood pressure?
bank.why: Methyldopa = Mom's drug: gestational hypertension and preeclampsia.

dw.Clonidine: Clonidine is an α2 agonist, but methyldopa is the one used in pregnancy.

bank.q: Which β1 agonist is used for cardiogenic shock and cardiac stress testing?
bank.why: Dobutamine (β1) DOBUles the heart's pumping.

dw.Dopamine: Dopamine acts on D1, β1 and α1.

bank.q: A student with asthma has an acute attack with wheezing. Which drug relieves the bronchospasm?
bank.why: Salbutamol (albuterol) is a β2 agonist (two lungs). Propranolol would make it worse.

bank.q: A woman at 30 weeks is in preterm labor. Which β2 agonist relaxes the uterus (tocolysis)?
bank.why: β2 agonists (salbutamol, terbutaline, isoxsuprine) relax smooth muscle of the lungs and uterus.

dw.Oxymetazoline: Oxymetazoline is an α agonist decongestant.

bank.q: Common side effects of salbutamol are...
bank.why: β2 agonists: tachycardia, tremors, nervousness, restlessness.

dw.Bradycardia and miosis: Bradycardia and miosis are not β2 effects.
dw.Dry cough and angioedema: Dry cough and angioedema are ACE-inhibitor effects.

bank.q: Isoproterenol is a...
d: Mixed α and β blocker (like labetalol)
bank.why: Isoproterenol acts on all β receptors; used for asthma.

bank.q: Norepinephrine is a strong β2 agonist.
bank.why: Norepinephrine: α1 > β1 >>> β2. It has very little β2 effect.

bank.q: A woman with episodes of palpitations, headache and excessive sweating has a pheochromocytoma. Which drug is given before surgery?
bank.why: PHEochromocytoma → PHEnoxybenzamine or PHEntolamine (nonselective α blockers). Pheo triad: palpitations, headache, excessive sweating.

dw.Propranolol: Propranolol alone can cause a hypertensive crisis in pheochromocytoma.

bank.q: Which α blocker binds irreversibly?
bank.why: Phenoxybenzamine = irreversible; phentolamine = reversible. Both nonselective.

dw.Phentolamine: Phentolamine is a reversible α blocker.
dw.Prazosin: Prazosin is a reversible α1 blocker.
dw.Tamsulosin: Tamsulosin is a reversible α1A blocker.

bank.q: Which nonselective α blocker is reversible?
bank.why: Phentolamine = reversible nonselective α blocker.

bank.q: Mang Lito, 65, has a weak urine stream from an enlarged prostate. Which drug relaxes the prostate and is the most prostate-selective?
bank.why: α1 blockers (-zosin: prazosin, doxazosin, tamsulosin) treat BPH; tamsulosin is the most prostate-selective. Pee-zosin.

bank.q: After his first dose of a new pill for BPH, Mr. Aquino nearly faints when he stands up. Which drug most likely caused it?
bank.why: α1 blockers cause orthostatic hypotension (vessels can't constrict on standing).

bank.q: Yohimbine is a(n)...
bank.why: Yohimbine blocks α2; obsolete; was used for orthostatic hypotension and erectile dysfunction.

dw.α1 agonist: Yohimbine is not an α1 agonist.
dw.β1 blocker: Yohimbine is not a β1 blocker.
dw.Muscarinic agonist: Yohimbine is not a muscarinic agonist.

bank.q: Which β-blocker is cardioselective (β1)?
bank.why: β1-selective = MANBABE: metoprolol, atenolol, nebivolol, bisoprolol, acebutolol, betaxolol, esmolol. Propranolol, timolol and pindolol are nonselective.

bank.q: Which β-blocker is NONselective?
bank.why: LOL trick: A–N = β1-selective; O–Z = nonselective (propranolol, timolol).
bank.hint: Starts with a letter after N.

bank.q: Which drug blocks both α and β receptors?
bank.why: Names ending in -lol but not -olol (labetalol, carvedilol) block α and β.

dw.Propranolol: Propranolol is a nonselective β-blocker only.

bank.q: Using the "LOL" trick, labetalol is...
bank.why: -lol but not -olol = α and β.

dw.An α2 agonist: Labetalol is not an α2 agonist.

bank.q: Which β-blocker is the shortest-acting and given IV?
bank.why: Esmolol: shortest-acting, IV (in MANBABE).

dw.Atenolol: Atenolol is a longer-acting oral drug.
dw.Propranolol: Propranolol is a longer-acting oral drug.
dw.Nebivolol: Nebivolol is a longer-acting oral drug.

bank.q: Which β-blocker is used to prevent migraine?
bank.why: Slides: propranolol for migraine prophylaxis (also hyperthyroidism).

dw.Esmolol: Esmolol is a short-acting IV drug.

bank.q: A hypertensive patient also has asthma. If a β-blocker must be used, which is the safer choice?
bank.why: Cardioselective (β1) blockers spare the β2 receptors in the lungs. Propranolol, timolol and pindolol block β2 and can trigger bronchospasm.

dw.Propranolol: Propranolol is nonselective and can cause bronchospasm.

bank.q: Which is NOT a β1-selective blocker (not in MANBABE)?
bank.why: MANBABE: metoprolol, atenolol, nebivolol, bisoprolol, acebutolol, betaxolol, esmolol.

bank.q: A woman with hyperthyroidism has palpitations and tremors. Which drug controls these symptoms?
bank.why: Slides: β-blockers are used in hyperthyroidism (and post-MI, hypertension, heart failure).

bank.q: Which is NOT a listed use of β-blockers?
bank.why: Uses: post-MI, hypertension, heart failure, hyperthyroidism, migraine. β-blockers can worsen asthma.

dw.Post-myocardial infarction: β-blockers are used after a myocardial infarction.
dw.Heart failure: β-blockers are used in heart failure.

bank.q: Tamsulosin is the α1 blocker most selective for the prostate.
bank.why: Slides: tamsulosin is the most prostate-selective -zosin.

bank.q: Atenolol is a nonselective β-blocker.
bank.why: Atenolol starts with A (A–N), so it's β1-selective (the A in MANBABE).

bank.q: Endocrine glands secrete their products...
bank.a: Directly into the blood as hormones
bank.why: Exocrine glands use ducts; endocrine glands release hormones into the blood.

dw.Onto the skin surface: Exocrine glands release onto the skin surface.
dw.Into the gut lumen only: Exocrine glands release into the gut lumen; endocrine glands use the blood.

bank.q: A hormone that acts on NEARBY cells is acting in a ___ manner.
bank.why: Circulating (endocrine) = far; paracrine = nearby cells; autocrine = the same cell.

dw.Autocrine: Autocrine acts on the same cell that released it.
dw.Endocrine: Endocrine acts at a distance through the blood.
dw.Exocrine: Exocrine release is through ducts, not a hormone action.

bank.q: Lipid-soluble hormones such as steroids and thyroid hormone act by...
bank.a: Entering the cell and binding a nuclear receptor to make new proteins
d: Binding a surface receptor and starting a second-messenger cascade
Staying in the blood without entering cells
bank.why: Lipid-soluble hormones cross the membrane → nuclear receptor → gene transcription. Water-soluble (amines, peptides) use surface receptors.

dw.Binding a surface receptor and starting: That is how peptide hormones act.
dw.Opening ion channels directly: Lipid-soluble hormones do not open ion channels directly.
dw.Staying in the blood without entering ce: They must enter cells to reach their receptors.

bank.q: In the thyroid axis, T3 and T4 inhibit TRH and TSH release. This is an example of...
bank.why: Hypothalamus TRH → pituitary TSH → thyroid T3/T4, which shuts down both.
bank.hint: The product turns off its own signal.

dw.Positive feedback: Positive feedback would amplify the signal.
dw.Autocrine signaling: Autocrine signaling acts on the releasing cell.
dw.Receptor desensitization: Desensitization is a change at the receptor.

bank.q: About 99% of the pancreas consists of...
bank.why: The pancreas is both exocrine (99% acini) and endocrine (islets scattered among the acini).

dw.Islets of Langerhans: The islets make up only about 1%.
dw.Beta cells: Beta cells are inside the islets, a small part.
dw.Ducts only: The pancreas has acini as well as ducts.

bank.q: Pancreatic alpha (A) cells secrete...
bank.why: Alpha (17%) = glucagon; beta (70%) = insulin; delta (7%) = somatostatin; F = pancreatic polypeptide.

bank.q: Which islet cells make insulin and are the largest share (about 70%)?
bank.why: Beta = biggest share, makes insulin.

bank.q: Delta (D) cells secrete...
bank.why: Delta (7%) = somatostatin.
bank.hint: The hormone that holds back both insulin and glucagon.

bank.q: F cells of the islets secrete...
bank.why: F cells = pancreatic polypeptide.

bank.q: Which is the hormone of the fasting state?
bank.why: Glucagon raises glucose during fasting by glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis.

dw.Insulin: Insulin is the hormone of the fed state.
dw.Somatostatin: Somatostatin is a general inhibitory hormone.
dw.Pancreatic polypeptide: Pancreatic polypeptide is not the fasting hormone.

bank.q: Which of these is a counterregulatory hormone (opposes insulin)?
bank.why: Counterregulatory: glucagon, growth hormone, cortisol, epinephrine (stress and fasting hormones).

bank.q: Insulin consists of...
bank.a: An A chain and a B chain joined by disulfide bridges
d: A single peptide chain with no disulfide bridges
A steroid ring made from cholesterol
bank.why: Proinsulin = A chain + B chain + C-peptide; the C-peptide is cut out.

dw.A single peptide chain with no disulfide: Insulin has two chains linked by disulfide bonds.
dw.Four identical subunits, like hemoglobin: Insulin is not a tetramer like hemoglobin.
dw.A steroid ring made from cholesterol: Insulin is a peptide, not a steroid.

bank.q: A patient may be secretly injecting insulin. Which lab marker shows whether high insulin comes from her own pancreas?
bank.why: C-peptide is cut from proinsulin, so it accompanies the body's own insulin; injected insulin has none. (Midterm true-or-false: C-peptide differentiates endogenous from exogenous insulin = True.)
bank.hint: The piece cut out of proinsulin.

dw.HbA1c: HbA1c reflects glucose control over about 3 months.
dw.Glucagon: Glucagon is not a marker of insulin origin.
dw.Fasting glucose: Fasting glucose does not distinguish the source.

bank.q: After glucose enters the β-cell through GLUT2 and ATP rises, what happens next?
bank.a: The ATP-sensitive K+ channel closes → depolarization → Ca2+ enters → insulin exocytosis
d: The K+ channel opens → hyperpolarization → insulin release stops
Ca2+ leaves the cell → insulin is released
Glucagon is released first, then insulin
bank.why: Sulfonylureas act on this same K+ channel to force insulin release.

dw.The K+ channel opens → hyperpolarization: Closing, not opening, of the K+ channel follows a rise in ATP.
dw.Ca2+ leaves the cell → insulin is releas: Ca2+ enters the cell; it does not leave.
dw.Glucagon is released first, then insulin: Insulin release is the response; glucagon is not first.

bank.q: Insulin makes muscle and fat take up glucose by moving which transporter to the cell membrane?
bank.why: GLUT-2 is the β-cell sensor; GLUT-4 is the insulin-responsive transporter of muscle and fat.

dw.GLUT-2: GLUT2 is in the β-cell and liver.
dw.SGLT2: SGLT2 is in the kidney tubule.
dw.NKCC2: NKCC2 is the loop diuretic target in the kidney.

bank.q: In the liver, insulin...
d: Increases ketone production from fatty acids
bank.why: Insulin stores fuel: ↑ glycogen and fat synthesis, ↓ glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis.

dw.Increases gluconeogenesis and glucose ou: Insulin decreases gluconeogenesis; glucagon increases it.
dw.Increases glycogenolysis and glucose rel: Insulin decreases glycogenolysis; glucagon increases it.

bank.q: In adipose tissue, insulin...
bank.a: Increases triglyceride storage and decreases lipolysis
d: Increases lipolysis and fatty acid release
Increases ketone release into the blood
bank.why: Insulin stores fat.

dw.Blocks glucose uptake through GLUT4: Insulin increases glucose uptake through GLUT4.

bank.q: The classic "3 Ps" of diabetes are...
bank.why: Appetite, thirst and urination.

dw.Polyphagia, pruritus and paresthesia: Pruritus and paresthesia are not the 3 Ps.
dw.Polyuria, proteinuria and polycythemia: Proteinuria and polycythemia are not the 3 Ps.

bank.q: Which is typical of type 1 diabetes?
bank.a: Autoimmune β-cell destruction; ketoacidosis is common
d: Insulin resistance in an obese adult
Treated first with diet, exercise and oral drugs
bank.why: Type 1: autoimmune, absolute insulin deficiency, usually < 30 years, thin, sudden, ketoacidosis common, 50% twin concordance.

dw.Insulin resistance in an obese adult: Insulin resistance in an obese adult is type 2.
dw.Gradual onset; 90% twin concordance: Gradual onset with 90% twin concordance is type 2.
dw.Treated first with diet, exercise and or: Diet, exercise and oral drugs first is the type 2 approach.

bank.q: Which is typical of type 2 diabetes?
bank.a: Insulin resistance with relative insulin deficiency
d: Insulin dependence from the very start
bank.why: Type 2: insulin resistance + relative deficiency, adults, often obese, ketoacidosis rare, 90% twin concordance. Type 2 is 90–95% of all diabetes.

dw.Frequent ketoacidosis, even without stre: Ketoacidosis is more typical of type 1.
dw.Insulin dependence from the very start: Type 2 is not insulin dependent from the start.

bank.q: The twin concordance of type 2 diabetes is about...
bank.why: Type 1 ~50%, type 2 ~90% (stronger genetics).

dw.50%: The concordance is higher than 50%: about 90%.
dw.10%: 10% is far too low; the concordance is about 90%.
dw.25%: 25% is too low; the concordance is about 90%.

bank.q: Which is a risk of gestational diabetes?
d: Lower risk of later type 2 diabetes
bank.why: Gestational DM risks: pre-eclampsia, macrosomia, cesarean delivery and later type 2 DM.

dw.A small, low-birth-weight baby: Gestational diabetes gives a larger baby, not a small one.
dw.Lower risk of later type 2 diabetes: It raises the risk of later type 2 diabetes.
dw.A shorter, easier labor: It makes delivery harder, not easier.

bank.q: Justyn: waist 105 cm, triglycerides 160 mg/dL, HDL 45 mg/dL, BP 128/82, fasting glucose 98 mg/dL. Does he have metabolic syndrome?
bank.a: No, only 2 of the 5 criteria are met
bank.why: Criteria (3 of 5 needed): waist ≥102 cm in men ✓; TG ≥150 ✓; HDL <40 in men ✗ (45); BP ≥130/85 ✗; fasting glucose ≥100 ✗. Only 2.

dw.Yes, 3 criteria are met: Only the waist and triglycerides meet cutoffs; HDL, BP and glucose do not, so 3 are not met.
dw.Yes, 4 criteria are met: Only 2 criteria are met, not 4: HDL 45, BP 128/82 and glucose 98 are all below the cutoffs.
dw.Yes, all 5 are met: Only 2 criteria are met, not all 5.

bank.q: Which patient meets the criteria for diabetes?
d: Josh: thirsty and urinating often, random glucose 199 mg/dL
bank.why: HbA1c ≥ 6.5% is diagnostic. A random glucose must be ≥200 with symptoms (199 is not), fasting must be ≥126. This mirrors the midterm item.

dw.Josh: thirsty and urinating often, rando: A random glucose of 199 is below 200, the cutoff for diabetes.
dw.Marti: fasting glucose 118 mg/dL: A fasting glucose of 118 is below 126, which is prediabetes.
dw.Dasha: HbA1c 6.2%: An HbA1c of 6.2% is below 6.5%, which is prediabetes.

bank.q: A fasting plasma glucose diagnostic of diabetes is...
bank.why: Fasting ≥126 mg/dL (7.0 mM). ≥100 is a metabolic syndrome criterion.

bank.q: A random plasma glucose diagnostic of diabetes (with symptoms) is...
bank.why: Random ≥200 with symptoms, or 2-h OGTT ≥200.

bank.q: An HbA1c diagnostic of diabetes is...
bank.why: HbA1c ≥ 6.5% diagnoses diabetes; the treatment target is < 7%.

bank.q: HbA1c reflects blood glucose control over the past...
bank.why: HbA1c follows the ~120-day lifespan of red blood cells.

dw.24 hours: 24 hours is too short for HbA1c.
dw.2 weeks: Two weeks is too short for HbA1c.

bank.q: What is the usual HbA1c target in diabetes management?
bank.why: Glycemic targets: HbA1c < 7%, relaxed to < 8% in the frail elderly.

dw.< 5.7%: That is the normal range, not the target for diabetes.
dw.< 6.5% for everyone: The target is below 7% for most people, not 6.5% for everyone.

bank.q: The pre-meal glucose target is...
bank.why: Pre-meal 90–130 mg/dL (5–7.2 mmol/L); 1-h postprandial < 180; 2-h postprandial < 150.

bank.q: The 2-hour postprandial glucose target is...
bank.why: 1-h postprandial < 180; 2-h postprandial < 150.

dw.< 180 mg/dL: Under 180 is too high for the target.
dw.< 200 mg/dL: Under 200 is too high for the target.

bank.q: The blood pressure target for diabetic patients in the lesson is...
bank.why: BP < 140/90 (the same number that starts treatment in the hypertension algorithm, Lesson 6).

dw.< 120/80 mmHg: That is the target for others, not the one in the lesson.

bank.q: A 60-kg patient with type 1 diabetes starts insulin. Using the lesson's rule, about how many units per day?
bank.why: Insulin units per day ≈ weight (kg) × 0.55 = 60 × 0.55 = 33.

dw.60 units: 60 units is a unit per kilogram, which is too much.
dw.27 units: 27 units is too low for the rule.

bank.q: What comes first in treating type 2 diabetes?
bank.a: Caloric restriction and more exercise, then metformin
bank.why: Type 2: lifestyle first, then metformin; add oral agents or insulin based on HbA1c.

dw.Insulin injections 3–4 times a day: Insulin is not the first step in type 2.
dw.A sulfonylurea before lifestyle changes: Lifestyle changes come before a sulfonylurea.

bank.q: Which fats are recommended in the diabetic diet?
d: Saturated animal fats (butter, lard, fatty meat)
Coconut and palm oils used for frying
bank.why: Mediterranean-style diet with monounsaturated fats.

dw.Saturated animal fats (butter, lard, fat: Saturated animal fats are not recommended.
dw.Coconut and palm oils used for frying: Coconut and palm oils are saturated fats.

bank.q: Which is a MACROvascular complication of diabetes?
bank.why: Micro = eyes, kidneys, nerves; macro = brain (stroke), heart (MI), legs (peripheral vascular disease).

bank.q: Which findings are signs of diabetic retinopathy?
d: Cataract and glaucoma, with no retinal changes
Blue sclera and a cherry-red spot
bank.why: Retinopathy: aneurysms, hemorrhages, cotton-wool spots.

dw.Cataract and glaucoma, with no retinal c: Cataract and glaucoma are not retinal changes of diabetes.
dw.Papilledema from raised intracranial pre: Papilledema comes from raised intracranial pressure.
dw.Blue sclera and a cherry-red spot: A cherry-red spot is a sign of other retinal disease.

bank.q: Where are incretins (GLP-1, GIP) made?
bank.why: Incretins are gut hormones released after an oral glucose load; they boost insulin and block glucagon. (Midterm item.)

dw.Pancreas: The pancreas makes insulin and glucagon.
dw.Liver: The liver does not make incretins.
dw.Kidney: The kidney does not make incretins.

bank.q: C-peptide can tell the body's own insulin from injected insulin.
bank.why: C-peptide is released with endogenous insulin; injected insulin contains none. (Midterm item.)

bank.q: Which insulin is RAPID-acting?
bank.why: Rapid = LAG: lispro, aspart, glulisine (onset 5–15 min). Glargine = long, NPH = intermediate, regular = short.

bank.q: Which insulin is given IV in emergencies such as diabetic ketoacidosis?
bank.why: Regular is the only one that goes Right into the vein.
bank.hint: R for right into the vein.

dw.NPH: NPH is a cloudy suspension and is not given IV.

bank.q: Which insulin lasts the longest (> 42 hours)?
bank.why: Long = GDD: glargine ~24 h, detemir 17 h, degludec > 42 h (De-gludec lasts De-cades).

bank.q: Which insulin has a flat profile with no peak?
bank.why: Long-acting analogs (glargine, detemir, degludec) are flat; NPH peaks at 6–7 h.

bank.q: NPH insulin is...
bank.why: NPH (neutral protamine Hagedorn): onset 2–4 h, peak 6–7 h, lasts 10–20 h.

dw.The only insulin given IV: Regular insulin is the one given IV.

bank.q: An insulin with onset 5–15 minutes, peak 1–1.5 hours, lasting 3–4 hours is...
bank.why: Those are the rapid-acting numbers; taken with meals.

dw.Short-acting (regular human insulin): Regular insulin has an onset of about 30 minutes.

bank.q: What is the most common side effect of insulin?
bank.why: Hypoglycemia: shaking, fast heart rate, hunger, sweating, confusion, dizziness.

dw.Lactic acidosis: Lactic acidosis is a metformin effect.
dw.Weight loss: Insulin causes weight gain, not loss.
dw.Genital infections: Genital infections come with SGLT2 inhibitors.

bank.q: Which is NOT a sign of hypoglycemia?
bank.why: Hypoglycemia: shaking, fast heart rate, hunger, sweating, confusion, dizziness. Polyuria is a sign of HIGH glucose.

dw.Sweating: Sweating is a sign of hypoglycemia.
dw.Shaking: Shaking is a sign of hypoglycemia.
dw.Confusion: Confusion is a sign of hypoglycemia.

bank.q: Which insulin combination mimics normal secretion in type 1 diabetes?
bank.a: Glargine once a day plus lispro with meals
d: NPH alone, once a day in the morning
Glipizide plus metformin, with no insulin
bank.why: Type 1: 3–4 injections a day; rapid + long-acting analogs (basal + mealtime). Glargine is the long-acting (basal) analog; lispro is the rapid-acting one taken with meals.

dw.NPH alone, once a day in the morning: NPH alone does not match mealtime needs.
dw.Regular insulin given IV only: Regular IV only is for emergencies.

bank.q: Detemir is a ___ insulin lasting about 17 hours.
bank.why: GDD: glargine, detemir, degludec are long-acting.

bank.q: Regular insulin is the insulin used IV in emergencies.
bank.why: Regular (short-acting) insulin is the one given IV.

bank.q: Which drug increases insulin release from the β-cells of the pancreas?
bank.why: Tolbutamide is a 1st-generation sulfonylurea: it closes the β-cell K+ channel to release insulin. Metformin (biguanide) lowers liver glucose output, miglitol (α-glucosidase inhibitor) slows carb digestion, pioglitazone (TZD) sensitizes tissues. Dr. Orig read this one out after the midterm.

bank.q: Kyle, a 60-year-old hypertensive and diabetic, was found confused and wandering around the house. She was also sweating and trembling. Which drug does she most likely take?
bank.why: Confusion + sweating + trembling = hypoglycemia. Glipizide (2nd-gen sulfonylurea) forces insulin release even when glucose is low. Exenatide (GLP-1 agonist) and sitagliptin (DPP-4 inhibitor) work only when glucose is high; rosiglitazone (TZD) is a sensitizer. Dr. Orig's own example from the midterm.
bank.hint: First name the problem (hypo- or hyperglycemia), then the class.

bank.q: Which drug is MOST likely to cause hypoglycemia when used alone?
bank.why: Sulfonylureas (glimepiride) cause hypoglycemia; metformin, acarbose and DPP-4 inhibitors rarely do on their own.
bank.hint: The one that squeezes the β-cell.

dw.Metformin: Metformin does not cause hypoglycemia alone.
dw.Acarbose: Acarbose does not cause hypoglycemia alone.

bank.q: Theresa takes a pill just before each meal; it works like a sulfonylurea but faster and shorter, to control post-meal glucose. Which drug is Theresa taking?
bank.why: Meglitinides (-glinide: repaglinide, mitiglinide) hit the same K+ channel as sulfonylureas with a faster onset and shorter action.

dw.Pioglitazone: Pioglitazone acts slowly on insulin sensitivity.
dw.Dapagliflozin: Dapagliflozin is an SGLT2 inhibitor taken daily.
dw.Insulin glargine: Insulin glargine is a long-acting injection.

bank.q: Sulfonylureas increase insulin release by...
bank.a: Closing the ATP-sensitive K+ channel of the β-cell
d: Activating AMPK in the liver (like metformin)
Binding PPAR-gamma in fat and muscle
Inhibiting DPP-4, so incretins last longer
bank.why: They block K+ efflux → depolarization → Ca2+ in → insulin out.

dw.Inhibiting DPP-4, so incretins last long: That is the DPP-4 inhibitors' action.

bank.q: Which is a FIRST-generation sulfonylurea?
bank.why: 1st gen (no longer used): tolbutamide, chlorpropamide, tolazamide. 2nd gen (more potent): glyburide, glipizide, glimepiride, gliclazide.

bank.q: Which is a SECOND-generation sulfonylurea?
bank.why: 2nd gen starts with gli- and ends in -ide.

bank.q: The major side effect of gliclazide is...
bank.why: Sulfonylureas: hypoglycemia (gliclazide is the slide's example) and weight gain.

dw.Lactic acidosis: Lactic acidosis is a metformin effect.
dw.Genital infections: Genital infections are an SGLT2 inhibitor effect.
dw.Flatulence: Flatulence is an alpha-glucosidase inhibitor effect.

bank.q: Glyburide belongs to which class?
bank.why: gli-…-ide = sulfonylurea.

bank.q: Mitiglinide belongs to which class?
bank.why: -glinide = meglitinide.

bank.q: Which drug activates AMPK to reduce glucose production by the liver?
bank.why: Metformin (biguanide) activates AMPK → ↓ hepatic glucose output.

bank.q: Which drug is first line for type 2 diabetes?
bank.why: Lifestyle, then metformin first.

dw.Insulin glargine: Insulin glargine is not first line in type 2.

bank.q: A woman with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) and insulin resistance is started on an antidiabetic drug. Which one?
bank.why: Metformin is also used in PCOS.

dw.Glipizide: Glipizide is a sulfonylurea; it is not used for PCOS.
dw.Exenatide: Exenatide is not the usual drug for PCOS.
dw.Acarbose: Acarbose is not the usual drug for PCOS.

bank.q: After years of diabetes treatment, Gian has numb feet and low vitamin B12. Which drug is the likely cause?
bank.why: Metformin SEs = GLB: GI upset, lactic acidosis, B12 deficiency.

dw.Glipizide: Glipizide is not linked to B12 deficiency.
dw.Sitagliptin: Sitagliptin is not linked to B12 deficiency.
dw.Canagliflozin: Canagliflozin is not linked to B12 deficiency.

bank.q: A diabetic patient with kidney failure develops lactic acidosis. Which drug is most likely responsible?
bank.why: Lactic acidosis is the L in metformin's GLB.

dw.Glimepiride: Glimepiride does not cause lactic acidosis.
dw.Linagliptin: Linagliptin does not cause lactic acidosis.
dw.Insulin lispro: Insulin lispro does not cause lactic acidosis.

bank.q: What is the most common side effect of metformin?
bank.why: GI effects are the most common; metformin alone doesn't cause hypoglycemia and is weight-neutral or causes loss.

dw.Weight gain from fat storage: Metformin does not cause weight gain.

bank.q: Which drug is a PPAR-gamma ligand that makes tissues respond better to insulin?
bank.why: Thiazolidinediones (-glitazone: pioglitazone, rosiglitazone) bind the nuclear receptor PPAR-gamma.

bank.q: A diabetic with heart failure gets worse leg swelling and breathlessness after a new antidiabetic drug. Which drug was most likely started?
bank.why: TZD SEs = FAB-W: fluid retention/heart failure, anemia, bone fractures, weight gain.

bank.q: A postmenopausal diabetic woman has a wrist fracture after a minor fall. Which of her drugs adds to bone loss?
bank.why: TZDs cause bone loss (fractures): the B in FAB-W.

dw.Metformin: Metformin does not add to bone loss.
dw.Glimepiride: Glimepiride does not add to bone loss.
dw.Linagliptin: Linagliptin does not add to bone loss.

bank.q: An obese diabetic wants a weekly injection that lowers glucose and body weight by acting like a gut hormone. Which drug fits?
bank.why: GLP-1 agonists (-glutide, exenatide) mimic the incretin GLP-1: more insulin, less glucagon, and weight loss.

bank.q: Weeks after starting an injectable antidiabetic, a patient has severe upper abdominal pain radiating to the back. Which drug is linked to acute pancreatitis?
bank.why: GLP-1 agonists: GI disturbances and acute pancreatitis.

dw.Metformin: Metformin is not linked to pancreatitis.
dw.Glyburide: Glyburide is not linked to pancreatitis.
dw.Acarbose: Acarbose is not linked to pancreatitis.

bank.q: Which drug inhibits the enzyme that breaks down incretins?
bank.why: DPP-4 inhibitors (-gliptin) keep the body's own incretins active. Exenatide is the GLP-1 agonist (look-alike trap).

dw.Exenatide: Exenatide is a GLP-1 agonist, not an enzyme inhibitor.

bank.q: Since starting a new oral antidiabetic, Harly has had a stuffy, sore nose and throat and headaches. Which drug is Harly most likely taking?
bank.why: DPP-4 inhibitors: headache, nasopharyngitis, upper respiratory infection.

bank.q: Which antidiabetic is weight NEUTRAL?
bank.why: Weight neutral: DPP-4 inhibitors and α-glucosidase inhibitors.

bank.q: Which drug lowers blood glucose by making the kidney excrete glucose in the urine?
bank.why: SGLT2 inhibitors (-gliflozin) block glucose reabsorption in the proximal tubule → glycosuria.

bank.q: A diabetic woman on a new drug has had two vaginal yeast infections and a UTI. Which drug is responsible?
bank.why: SGLT2 inhibitors: sugary urine → genital and urinary tract infections.

dw.Metformin: Metformin does not cause genital infections.
dw.Glimepiride: Glimepiride does not cause genital infections.
dw.Sitagliptin: Sitagliptin does not cause genital infections.

bank.q: Which drug inhibits intestinal alpha-glucosidase?
bank.why: Acarbose and miglitol slow starch and disaccharide digestion → smaller post-meal spikes.

bank.q: After starting a drug that lowers his after-meal sugar, Mr. Dela Cruz complains of bloating and flatulence. Which drug is he most likely taking?
bank.why: α-glucosidase inhibitors: undigested carbs reach the colon and ferment → gas, diarrhea, abdominal pain.

bank.q: Which antidiabetic causes WEIGHT GAIN?
bank.why: Gain: insulin, sulfonylureas, meglitinides, TZDs. Loss: metformin, SGLT2 inhibitors, GLP-1 agonists, pramlintide.

dw.Metformin: Metformin is weight neutral or causes loss.

bank.q: Which antidiabetic causes WEIGHT LOSS?
bank.why: SGLT2 inhibitors dump sugar (calories) in the urine → weight loss.

bank.q: Pramlintide is listed in which weight group?
bank.why: Weight loss: GLP-1 agonists, metformin, SGLT2 inhibitors, pramlintide.

dw.Weight gain: Pramlintide is not in the weight gain group.
dw.Weight neutral: Pramlintide is not in the weight neutral group.

bank.q: Which drug is NOT a DPP-4 inhibitor?
bank.why: DPP-4 inhibitors end in -gliptin. Exenatide is a GLP-1 agonist.

bank.q: Which drug is NOT a GLP-1 receptor agonist?
bank.why: GLP-1 agonists end in -glutide (or exenatide). Saxagliptin is a DPP-4 inhibitor.

bank.q: Which drug is NOT an SGLT2 inhibitor?
bank.why: -gliflozin = SGLT2; -gliptin = DPP-4.

bank.q: Which drug is NOT a sulfonylurea?
bank.why: Repaglinide is a meglitinide (-glinide), though it acts on the same K+ channel.

bank.q: GLP-1 agonists lower glucose mainly by...
bank.a: Increasing insulin release and suppressing glucagon
d: Blocking glucose reabsorption in the kidney
Slowing starch digestion in the gut
bank.why: They act like the incretin GLP-1 after a meal. (Also slow gastric emptying and reduce appetite.)

dw.Blocking glucose reabsorption in the kid: That is how SGLT2 inhibitors work.
dw.Slowing starch digestion in the gut: That is how alpha-glucosidase inhibitors work.

bank.q: Octreotide was used to treat a patient's hypoglycemia. Which antidiabetic was the patient most likely taking?
bank.why: Octreotide is the antidote for sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycemia; glyburide is a sulfonylurea. (Midterm item.)

bank.q: Which antidiabetic class is in the CYP INDUCER mnemonic (BULLSHIT CRAP GP'S)?
bank.why: The final S in GP'S = sulfonylureas. Midterm: "Glipizide is a CYP inducer".

dw.Biguanides, e.g. metformin: Biguanides are not in the inducer mnemonic.
dw.DPP-4 inhibitors, e.g. sitagliptin: DPP-4 inhibitors are not in the inducer mnemonic.
dw.SGLT2 inhibitors, e.g. dapagliflozin: SGLT2 inhibitors are not in the inducer mnemonic.

bank.q: Metformin used alone does not usually cause hypoglycemia.
bank.why: Metformin lowers liver glucose output without forcing insulin release.

bank.q: Alpha-glucosidase inhibitors lower fasting blood glucose.
bank.why: They only blunt post-meal spikes; they have no effect on fasting glucose.

bank.q: Sitagliptin causes weight loss.
bank.why: DPP-4 inhibitors are weight neutral; GLP-1 agonists cause weight loss.

bank.q: Blood pressure equals...
bank.why: BP = CO × SVR, and CO = HR × SV. Every antihypertensive lowers one of these (or the blood volume behind CO).

dw.Heart rate × stroke volume: That's cardiac output (CO = HR × SV). BP takes CO one step further: CO × SVR.
dw.Stroke volume × systemic vascular resist: It leaves out heart rate. BP = CO × SVR, and CO needs both HR and SV.
dw.Cardiac output ÷ systemic vascular resis: Resistance RAISES pressure, so it multiplies: BP = CO × SVR.

bank.q: Cardiac output equals...
bank.why: CO = HR × SV.

dw.Blood pressure × resistance: Pressure and resistance give BP's own formula (BP = CO × SVR), not CO.
dw.Stroke volume ÷ heart rate: Each beat's volume is multiplied by the beats per minute: CO = HR × SV.
dw.Heart rate × systemic vascular resistanc: SVR belongs to the BP formula. CO = HR × stroke volume.

bank.q: Systolic blood pressure is the pressure in the arteries...
d: When the heart is relaxed between beats
bank.why: Systolic = upper number, during contraction (at the heartbeat); diastolic = lower number, heart relaxed.

dw.When the heart is relaxed between beats: That's diastolic pressure, the lower number.
dw.In the veins during inspiration: Systolic and diastolic are ARTERIAL pressures.
dw.Averaged over one minute: An average over the cycle is the mean arterial pressure. Systolic is the peak, during contraction.

bank.q: In a reading of 150/90, the 90 is the...
bank.a: Diastolic pressure, while the heart is relaxed
d: Systolic pressure, while the heart contracts
bank.why: Lower number = diastolic, between beats.

dw.Systolic pressure, while the heart contr: Systolic is the UPPER number (150 here).
dw.Mean arterial pressure: MAP is calculated from both numbers; it isn't either number of the reading.
dw.Pulse pressure: Pulse pressure is the difference between the two numbers (150 − 90 = 60).

bank.q: Which INCREASES systemic vascular resistance?
bank.why: SVR rises with higher viscosity (polycythemia), longer total vessel length (obesity) and smaller radius (vasoconstriction).

dw.Fewer red blood cells (anemia): Fewer RBCs make the blood thinner, so viscosity and SVR go DOWN.
dw.Weight loss: Less body mass means less total vessel length, so SVR goes down.

bank.q: Polycythemia raises blood pressure mainly by increasing...
bank.why: More RBCs → thicker blood → more resistance.

dw.Heart rate: Extra RBCs don't speed the heart; they thicken the blood.
dw.Total vessel length: Vessel length goes up with obesity, not polycythemia.
dw.Venous return only: The key change is thicker blood (viscosity), which raises SVR.

bank.q: Obesity raises SVR mainly by increasing...
bank.why: A bigger body needs more vessels → longer total length → more resistance.

dw.Blood viscosity: Viscosity rises with polycythemia (more RBCs), not with body size.
dw.Vessel radius: Radius changes with vasoconstriction or dilation. Obesity adds more vessels (length).
dw.Parasympathetic tone: Parasympathetic tone affects heart rate, not resistance from extra vessels.

bank.q: Which raises heart rate?
bank.a: Increased sympathetic impulses and adrenal medulla hormones
d: Increased parasympathetic impulses from the vagus nerve
Acetylcholine acting on M2 receptors in the SA node
Atrial natriuretic peptide released by the atria
bank.why: ↓ parasympathetic or ↑ sympathetic (and adrenal epinephrine) → ↑ HR → ↑ CO.

dw.Acetylcholine acting on M2 receptors in: M2 in the SA node is the parasympathetic brake: it slows the heart.
dw.Atrial natriuretic peptide released by t: ANP lowers blood volume (sodium loss); it doesn't speed the heart.

bank.q: Which does NOT increase venous return?
bank.why: Venous return rises with blood volume, the muscle and respiratory pumps, and VENOconstriction.
bank.hint: Which one pools blood in the veins?

dw.Skeletal muscle pump: Contracting leg muscles squeeze blood back to the heart, so venous return INCREASES.
dw.Respiratory pump: Breathing pressure changes pull blood toward the heart, so venous return INCREASES.
dw.Increased blood volume: More volume means more blood coming back, so venous return INCREASES.

bank.q: Which hormone LOWERS blood pressure?
bank.why: ANP vasodilates and lowers blood volume. Angiotensin II, aldosterone and ADH all raise BP.

bank.q: Which hormone raises BP by increasing blood volume?
bank.why: Blood volume ↑: aldosterone, ADH. Blood volume ↓: ANP.

dw.Atrial natriuretic peptide: ANP makes the kidneys lose sodium and water, so it LOWERS blood volume.
dw.Nitric oxide: NO is a vasodilator; it lowers BP and doesn't change volume.
dw.Epinephrine: Epinephrine raises BP through the heart (β1) and vessels, not through blood volume.

bank.q: Which substance lowers BP by vasodilation?
bank.why: Vasodilators in Table 21.2: ANP, epinephrine (β2), nitric oxide.

bank.q: Epinephrine dilates the arterioles of skeletal and cardiac muscle through...
bank.why: Table footnote: epinephrine acts at β2 in cardiac and skeletal muscle arterioles; at α1 elsewhere it constricts.

bank.q: Which is NOT one of the four anatomic sites of blood pressure control?
bank.why: Four sites: arterioles (resistance), venules (capacitance), heart (pump output), kidneys (volume).

bank.q: Which vessels are the RESISTANCE vessels in BP control?
bank.why: Arterioles = resistance; venules = capacitance.

bank.q: Which vessels are the CAPACITANCE vessels?
bank.why: Venules hold (store) blood = capacitance.

bank.q: The kidneys control blood pressure mainly through...
bank.a: Blood volume, via renin → angiotensin → aldosterone
d: Heart rate, via signals to the SA node
Blood viscosity, via red cell production
Vessel length, via new blood vessel growth
bank.why: Site 4: kidneys = volume control (RAAS).

bank.q: Hypertension is diagnosed based on...
bank.a: Repeated, reproducible measurements of elevated BP
d: One high reading taken during a clinic visit
A single high reading from a home monitor
Symptoms such as headache and nosebleeds
bank.why: Slides: repeated, reproducible measurements.

dw.One high reading taken during a clinic v: One reading can be stress or white-coat. The diagnosis needs REPEATED readings.
dw.A single high reading from a home monito: A single reading isn't enough; it must be repeated and reproducible.
dw.Symptoms such as headache and nosebleeds: Hypertension is usually silent. It's diagnosed by measurement, not symptoms.

bank.q: Hypertension with no specific cause is called...
bank.why: Primary (essential) = no specific cause; secondary = specific etiology.

dw.Secondary hypertension: Secondary means there IS a specific cause (e.g. pheochromocytoma).
dw.Resistant hypertension: Resistant = uncontrolled on 3 drugs including a diuretic. It's about treatment, not cause.
dw.Hypertensive crisis: A crisis is a level (above 180 and/or above 120), not a type by cause.

bank.q: Hypertension caused by a pheochromocytoma is...
bank.why: It has a specific etiology, so it's secondary.

dw.Primary (essential) hypertension: Primary means NO known cause. A pheochromocytoma is a known cause.
dw.Resistant hypertension: Resistant = uncontrolled on 3 drugs including a diuretic. It doesn't describe the cause.
dw.Elevated blood pressure: Elevated is a reading category (120–129 and < 80), not a cause.

bank.q: Sophia's repeated readings average 125/78 mmHg. How is this classified?
bank.why: Elevated = 120–129 AND below 80.

dw.Normal: Normal needs BOTH below 120 AND below 80; a systolic of 125 is not below it.
dw.Hypertension stage 1: Stage 1 needs a systolic of 130–139 OR a diastolic of 80–89; 125/78 has neither.
dw.Hypertension stage 2: Stage 2 needs a systolic of 140 or more, OR a diastolic of 90 or more; 125/78 reaches neither.

bank.q: Abdel's repeated readings average 135/85 mmHg. How is this classified?

dw.Elevated: Elevated needs the diastolic BELOW 80 (it uses AND). A diastolic of 85 already counts as stage 1 (80–89).
dw.Hypertension stage 2: Stage 2 needs a systolic of 140 or more, OR a diastolic of 90 or more; 135/85 reaches neither.
dw.Normal: Normal needs BOTH below 120 AND below 80; a systolic of 135 and a diastolic of 85 are not below them.

bank.q: Keisha's readings average 125/85 mmHg. How is this classified?
bank.why: Elevated needs systolic 120–129 AND diastolic < 80. A diastolic of 85 is in the 80–89 range, and stage 1 needs only one number (OR).

dw.Elevated: Elevated needs the diastolic BELOW 80 (it uses AND). A diastolic of 85 already counts as stage 1 (80–89).
dw.Normal: Normal needs BOTH below 120 AND below 80; a systolic of 125 and a diastolic of 85 are not below them.
dw.Hypertension stage 2: Stage 2 needs a systolic of 140 or more, OR a diastolic of 90 or more; 125/85 reaches neither.

bank.q: Gabriel's readings average 118/92 mmHg. How is this classified?
bank.why: Stage 2 = ≥140 OR ≥90. A diastolic of 92 alone makes it stage 2.

dw.Normal: Normal needs BOTH below 120 AND below 80; a diastolic of 92 is not below it.
dw.Elevated: Elevated needs the diastolic BELOW 80 (it uses AND). A diastolic of 92 already counts as stage 2 (≥ 90).
dw.Hypertension stage 1: Stage 1 is 130–139 OR 80–89, but the diastolic 92 reaches stage 2, and the higher category wins.

bank.q: Niña's BP is 190/110 mmHg. How is this classified?
bank.why: Crisis = above 180 and/or above 120. Systolic 190 qualifies.

dw.Hypertension stage 1: Stage 1 is 130–139 OR 80–89, but the systolic 190 reaches hypertensive crisis, and the higher category wins.
dw.Hypertension stage 2: 190/110 goes ABOVE 180, which makes it a crisis, past stage 2.
dw.Elevated: Elevated needs the diastolic BELOW 80 (it uses AND). A diastolic of 110 already counts as stage 2 (≥ 90).

bank.q: Josef's repeated readings of 150/95 mmHg are classified as...
bank.why: Stage 2 = ≥140 or ≥90.

dw.Hypertension stage 1: Stage 1 is 130–139 OR 80–89, but the systolic 150 reaches stage 2, and the higher category wins.
dw.Elevated: Elevated needs the diastolic BELOW 80 (it uses AND). A diastolic of 95 already counts as stage 2 (≥ 90).
dw.Hypertensive crisis: A crisis needs a systolic ABOVE 180 or a diastolic ABOVE 120; 150/95 has neither.

bank.q: Frances's repeated readings of 119/79 mmHg are classified as...
bank.why: Normal = below 120 AND below 80.

dw.Elevated: Elevated starts at a systolic of 120; 119 is still normal.
dw.Hypertension stage 1: Stage 1 needs a systolic of 130–139 OR a diastolic of 80–89; 119/79 has neither.
dw.Hypertension stage 2: Stage 2 needs a systolic of 140 or more, OR a diastolic of 90 or more; 119/79 reaches neither.

bank.q: To be classified as "Elevated", BOTH the systolic must be 120–129 AND the diastolic below 80.
bank.why: Normal and Elevated use AND; stages 1 and 2 use OR (either number).

bank.q: Diuretics lower blood pressure mainly by...
d: Blocking β1 receptors in the heart
bank.why: Slides: diuretics lower BP by depleting body sodium stores.

dw.Releasing nitric oxide: That's how vasodilators like hydralazine and nitroprusside work.

bank.q: In most patients, diuretics lower BP by about...
bank.why: Slides: 10–15 mmHg; used alone in mild or moderate essential hypertension.

dw.1–2 mmHg: Too small; that wouldn't be worth treating with. The slide says 10–15.
dw.40–50 mmHg: Too large for one diuretic; the slide says 10–15.
dw.80–100 mmHg: No single drug lowers BP that much; the slide says 10–15.

bank.q: Diuretics may be used ALONE in...
d: Every stage 2 patient, whatever the risk
bank.why: Slides: used alone in mild or moderate essential hypertension.

dw.Hypertensive crisis with organ damage: A crisis needs fast IV drugs, not a diuretic alone.
dw.Resistant hypertension on three drugs: Resistant means already uncontrolled on 3 drugs, so one diuretic won't do.
dw.Every stage 2 patient, whatever the risk: Alone, a diuretic is for MILD or moderate essential hypertension only.

bank.q: Acetazolamide acts at the...
bank.why: Sites in nephron order: acetazolamide (PCT), osmotic (PCT + descending limb), loop (TAL), thiazide (DCT), K-sparing (collecting duct). A-O-L-T-K.

bank.q: Acetazolamide is a...
bank.why: Acetazolamide = carbonic anhydrase inhibitor at the PCT.

bank.q: Which is an osmotic diuretic?
bank.why: Mannitol (osmotic) acts at the PCT and descending limb.

bank.q: Which diuretic acts on the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle?
bank.why: Loop diuretics (furosemide, torsemide, bumetanide, ethacrynic acid) act in the TAL.

dw.Hydrochlorothiazide: Thiazide, so it acts in the DCT.
dw.Spironolactone: K-sparing (aldosterone antagonist), so it acts in the collecting duct.
dw.Acetazolamide: Carbonic anhydrase inhibitor, so it acts in the proximal tubule.

bank.q: Which diuretic acts on the distal convoluted tubule?
bank.why: Thiazides (HCTZ, chlorthalidone, metolazone) block NCC in the DCT.
bank.hint: T for thiazide, T for disTal.

dw.Furosemide: Loop diuretic, so it acts in the thick ascending limb.
dw.Amiloride: K-sparing (ENaC blocker), so it acts in the collecting duct.
dw.Mannitol: Osmotic diuretic, so it acts where water moves (proximal tubule and loop), not by blocking a DCT transporter.

bank.q: Which diuretic acts in the collecting duct?
bank.why: K-sparing diuretics (spironolactone, eplerenone, amiloride, triamterene) act in the collecting tubule/duct.

dw.Furosemide: Loop diuretic, so it acts in the thick ascending limb.
dw.Chlorthalidone: Thiazide-like, so it acts in the DCT.
dw.Acetazolamide: Carbonic anhydrase inhibitor, so it acts in the proximal tubule.

bank.q: Which drug inhibits NKCC2, the Na+/K+/2Cl− cotransporter?
bank.why: Loop diuretics block NKCC2 in the TAL. Metolazone = thiazide-like (NCC), eplerenone and triamterene = K-sparing.

dw.Metolazone: Thiazide-like: it blocks NCC in the DCT.
dw.Eplerenone: K-sparing: it blocks the aldosterone receptor.
dw.Triamterene: K-sparing: it blocks ENaC in the collecting duct.

bank.q: Which drug blocks the Na+/Cl− cotransporter (NCC) in the DCT?
bank.why: Thiazides and thiazide-like drugs (chlorthalidone, indapamide, metolazone) block NCC.

dw.Torsemide: Loop diuretic: it blocks NKCC2 in the TAL.
dw.Spironolactone: K-sparing: it blocks the aldosterone receptor.
dw.Amiloride: K-sparing: it blocks ENaC in the collecting duct.

bank.q: Which drug blocks the epithelial Na+ channel (ENaC)?
bank.why: ENaC inhibitors: amiloride, triamterene. Spironolactone blocks the aldosterone receptor instead.
bank.hint: A potassium-sparing diuretic that doesn't touch the aldosterone receptor.

dw.Spironolactone: Also K-sparing, but it blocks the aldosterone RECEPTOR, not the channel.

bank.q: Which drug blocks the aldosterone (mineralocorticoid) receptor?
bank.why: Aldosterone antagonists: spironolactone, eplerenone.

dw.Triamterene: Also K-sparing, but it blocks ENaC directly.
dw.Hydrochlorothiazide: Thiazide: it blocks NCC.

bank.q: The two PROTOTYPE loop diuretics on the slide are...
bank.why: Slide: 2 prototype drugs, furosemide and ethacrynic acid; bumetanide and torsemide are the others.

dw.Bumetanide and torsemide: They are loop diuretics too, but not the two prototypes on the slide.

bank.q: Steve has acute pulmonary edema: severe breathlessness and crackles in both lungs. Which diuretic is used?
bank.why: Loop diuretics: acute pulmonary edema and other edematous conditions (the strongest diuretics).

dw.Hydrochlorothiazide: Thiazides are too weak for an emergency; they're for hypertension.
dw.Spironolactone: K-sparing diuretics are weak; they're for hyperaldosteronism and heart failure.
dw.Acetazolamide: A carbonic anhydrase inhibitor, for glaucoma and altitude sickness.

bank.q: Dinniella's serum K+ is dangerously high. Which diuretic helps remove K+?
bank.why: Loop diuretics are used for hyperkalemia (they waste K+). K-sparing diuretics would raise K+ further.

dw.Spironolactone: K-sparing: it KEEPS K+, so it would make her worse.

bank.q: Which is NOT a listed use of loop diuretics?
bank.why: Loop uses: pulmonary edema/edema, hyperkalemia, acute renal failure. Hyperaldosteronism is a K-sparing (spironolactone) use.

dw.Acute pulmonary edema: That's the number one loop use.
dw.Hyperkalemia: It IS a loop use: loops waste K+.
dw.Acute renal failure: It IS on the loop list (to move the fluid out).

bank.q: Julianne, on IV diuretics for heart failure, complains of ringing in the ears and hearing loss. Which drug is causing this?
bank.why: Loop diuretic toxicity: ototoxicity and allergic reactions. The ear has a loop too.

dw.Hydrochlorothiazide: Thiazide toxicity is LUNA (lipids, uric acid, Na+ down, allergy), not the ear.
dw.Spironolactone: Spironolactone causes hyperkalemia and gynecomastia, not ear damage.

bank.q: The usual total daily oral dose of furosemide is...
bank.why: Table 15-4: bumetanide 0.5–2 mg, torsemide 5–20 mg, furosemide 20–80 mg, ethacrynic acid 50–200 mg.

bank.q: Which loop diuretic has the smallest daily dose (0.5–2 mg)?
bank.why: Bumetanide is the most potent per mg.

dw.Furosemide: Furosemide needs more mg than bumetanide; bumetanide is the most potent per mg.
dw.Torsemide: Torsemide also needs more mg than bumetanide.
dw.Ethacrynic acid: Ethacrynic acid needs the LARGEST dose (50–200 mg).

bank.q: Which loop diuretic has the largest daily dose (50–200 mg)?
bank.why: Ethacrynic acid 50–200 mg.

dw.Bumetanide: Bumetanide has the SMALLEST dose (0.5–2 mg).
dw.Torsemide: Torsemide works at a much smaller dose than ethacrynic acid.
dw.Furosemide: Furosemide is in the middle; ethacrynic acid needs the most.

bank.q: What is the prototype thiazide diuretic?
bank.why: Slide: prototype drug, hydrochlorothiazide.

bank.q: Thiazide diuretics are used for...
bank.why: Slides: thiazide uses = hypertension, heart failure.

dw.Glaucoma and altitude sickness: Those are acetazolamide (carbonic anhydrase inhibitor) uses.

bank.q: Two months after starting a diuretic for hypertension, Ron has a hot, swollen, painful big toe (gout). Which diuretic is Ron most likely taking?
bank.why: Thiazide toxicity = LUNA: Lipids up, Uric acid up (gout), Na+ down, Allergy.

dw.Spironolactone: Spironolactone causes hyperkalemia and gynecomastia, not gout.
dw.Losartan: An ARB, not a diuretic. It actually lowers uric acid a little.

bank.q: Which is NOT a listed toxicity of thiazide diuretics?
bank.why: Thiazide toxicity: hyperlipidemia, hyponatremia, gout, allergic reactions. Hyperkalemia is the K-sparing diuretics' problem.

dw.Hyperlipidemia: It IS a thiazide toxicity (the L in LUNA).
dw.Hyponatremia: It IS a thiazide toxicity (the Na in LUNA).
dw.Gout: It IS a thiazide toxicity (the U, uric acid, in LUNA).

bank.q: Which drug is NOT a true thiazide but a sulfonamide that acts like one?
bank.why: Thiazide-like (footnote 1): chlorthalidone, indapamide, metolazone, quinethazone.

bank.q: Which thiazide is given in TWO divided doses?
bank.why: Table 15-6: chlorothiazide (0.5–2 g) and hydroflumethiazide are twice daily; the rest once daily.

bank.q: The daily dose of hydrochlorothiazide in Table 15-6 is...
bank.why: HCTZ 25–100 mg once daily.

bank.q: Potassium-sparing diuretics work by...
bank.a: Countering aldosterone in the collecting tubules
d: Blocking NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb
Blocking NCC in the distal tubule
Inhibiting carbonic anhydrase in the proximal tubule
bank.why: Slide wording. Two groups: aldosterone antagonists (spironolactone, eplerenone) and ENaC inhibitors (amiloride, triamterene). Either way, less K+ is secreted, so potassium is spared.

bank.q: Carylle has primary hyperaldosteronism with high BP and low K+. Which diuretic fits best?
bank.why: K-sparing uses: hyperaldosteronism, heart failure. Loops and thiazides would lower K+ further.

dw.Furosemide: A loop wastes K+, and her K+ is already low.
dw.Hydrochlorothiazide: Thiazides also lower K+, so they'd worsen her hypokalemia.
dw.Acetazolamide: It's for glaucoma and altitude sickness, and it also lowers K+.

bank.q: Mr. Domingo, on a diuretic for heart failure, notices tender breast enlargement. Which diuretic is he most likely taking?
bank.why: Spironolactone toxicity: hyperkalemia and gynecomastia (it's a steroid look-alike).

dw.Furosemide: Loop toxicity is ototoxicity and allergy, not gynecomastia.
dw.Hydrochlorothiazide: Thiazide toxicity is LUNA, not gynecomastia.
dw.Amiloride: Amiloride is K-sparing but not a steroid look-alike, so no gynecomastia.

bank.q: Which diuretic can cause HYPERkalemia?
bank.why: K-sparing diuretics (triamterene, amiloride, spironolactone, eplerenone) keep K+ in.

dw.Hydrochlorothiazide: A thiazide: it LOWERS K+.

bank.q: Which list follows the nephron in order of the diuretics' sites, from first to last?
bank.why: A-O-L-T-K: All Our Loops Take K+.

bank.q: Which statement correctly compares loop and thiazide diuretics?
bank.a: Loops block NKCC2 in the TAL; thiazides block NCC in the DCT
d: Loops block NCC in the DCT; thiazides block NKCC2 in the TAL
Both block ENaC in the collecting duct
bank.why: Loop = NKCC2/TAL (strongest, for edema); thiazide = NCC/DCT (for hypertension).

dw.Loops block NCC in the DCT; thiazides bl: Swapped. Loops are in the LOOP (TAL, NKCC2).
dw.Both block ENaC in the collecting duct: ENaC is the K-sparing drugs' target (amiloride, triamterene).

bank.q: Loop diuretics act on the distal convoluted tubule.
bank.why: Loop diuretics act on the thick ascending limb (NKCC2); thiazides act on the DCT.

bank.q: Spironolactone causes hypokalemia.
bank.why: Spironolactone spares K+, so it causes HYPERkalemia.

bank.q: Thiazide diuretics are first-line drugs for hypertension.
bank.why: Thiazides are among the four first-line classes (ACEi, ARB, CCB, thiazide).

bank.q: Which drug is NOT a sympatholytic antihypertensive?
bank.why: Sympatholytics: methyldopa, clonidine, β-blockers, prazosin and α1 blockers, phentolamine/phenoxybenzamine. Hydralazine is a direct vasodilator.
bank.hint: Which one acts directly on the vessel?

dw.Methyldopa: It IS a sympatholytic (central α2 agonist).
dw.Clonidine: It IS a sympatholytic (central α2 agonist).

bank.q: Sympathetic discharge raises blood pressure through...
bank.a: α1 receptors on vessels and β1 receptors on the heart
d: β2 receptors on vessels and M2 receptors on the heart
α2 receptors on vessels and β2 receptors on the heart
Nicotinic receptors on vessels and the kidney
bank.why: Slide diagram: α1 → vasoconstriction; β1 → ↑ rate and force (↑ afterload) → ↑ BP.

dw.β2 receptors on vessels and M2 receptors: β2 RELAXES vessels, and M2 is the parasympathetic brake.
dw.α2 receptors on vessels and β2 receptors: α2 is the presynaptic brake, and the heart's receptor is β1.
dw.Nicotinic receptors on vessels and the k: Nicotinic receptors are at ganglia and muscle, not the vessel wall.

bank.q: Blocking which receptor lowers BP by reducing heart rate and force?
bank.why: β-blockers block β1 on the heart.

dw.α2: α2 blockade would RAISE sympathetic outflow (it releases the brake).
dw.β2: β2 is in the lungs and vessels; blocking it causes bronchospasm.
dw.M3: M3 is a muscarinic (parasympathetic) receptor on glands and smooth muscle.

bank.q: Which antihypertensive acts in the brain to lower sympathetic outflow and is the classic choice in pregnancy?
bank.why: Methyldopa (central α2 agonist) = Mom's drug. ACE inhibitors and ARBs are contraindicated in pregnancy.

dw.Spironolactone: A K-sparing diuretic, not a central drug.

bank.q: Justyn stopped his blood pressure pills suddenly and his BP shot up within a day (rebound hypertension). Which drug is known for this?
bank.why: Textbook extra (not on the slides): abrupt withdrawal of clonidine causes rebound hypertension.

bank.q: Methyldopa and clonidine lower BP by...
bank.a: Stimulating α2 receptors in the brainstem
d: Blocking α1 receptors on blood vessels
Blocking β1 receptors in the heart
Releasing nitric oxide in the vessel wall
bank.why: Both are α2 agonists (Lesson 4). Stimulating central α2 receptors lowers sympathetic outflow from the brain.

bank.q: Mang Lito has hypertension and an enlarged prostate. Which drug can help both?
bank.why: α1 blockers (-zosin) relax vessels and the prostate. (Tamsulosin is the most prostate-selective, with the least BP effect.)

dw.Atenolol: A β1 blocker: no effect on the prostate.
dw.Hydrochlorothiazide: A thiazide: it would make him urinate more, which won't help the prostate.
dw.Losartan: An ARB: no effect on the prostate.

bank.q: Which vasodilator is given ORALLY?
bank.why: Oral: hydralazine, minoxidil. Parenteral: nitroprusside, fenoldopam.
bank.hint: Nitroprusside and fenoldopam are IV drips; esmolol is a short-acting IV β-blocker.

dw.Esmolol: An IV short-acting β1 blocker, not a vasodilator.

bank.q: Which vasodilator is given PARENTERALLY (IV)?
bank.why: Parenteral: nitroprusside, fenoldopam.

dw.Amlodipine: An oral CCB.

bank.q: Which vasodilator works by releasing nitric oxide?
bank.why: Table 11-3: NO release = nitroprusside, hydralazine, nitrates, histamine, acetylcholine. Minoxidil opens K+ channels; fenoldopam hits dopamine receptors; verapamil blocks Ca2+.

bank.q: Which drug lowers BP by opening K+ channels and hyperpolarizing smooth muscle?
bank.why: Hyperpolarization via K+ channels: minoxidil, diazoxide.
bank.hint: Mino and Dia open the K+ door.

bank.q: Diazoxide lowers BP by...
bank.why: Minoxidil and diazoxide = K+ channel openers.

bank.q: Which vasodilator activates dopamine receptors?
bank.why: Fenol-DOPA-m acts on DOPAmine (D1) receptors.

dw.Nifedipine: A CCB: it blocks Ca2+ influx.

bank.q: Which antihypertensive is sold as a 5% topical solution for hair regrowth?
bank.why: The slide shows topical minoxidil 5% (Regroe): its hair-growth side effect became a hair-regrowth product.

bank.q: Calcium channel blockers lower BP by...
bank.a: Inhibiting Ca2+ influx into arterial smooth muscle cells
d: Opening K+ channels in arterial smooth muscle
Releasing nitric oxide from the endothelium
Blocking AT1 receptors on vascular smooth muscle
bank.why: Slide MOA: inhibition of Ca2+ influx into arterial smooth muscle.

bank.q: Which is a DIHYDROPYRIDINE calcium channel blocker?
bank.why: Dihydropyridines end in -dipine (amlodipine, felodipine, nifedipine, nicardipine). Verapamil and diltiazem are non-dihydropyridines.

bank.q: Marielle, who is hypertensive with a fast heart rate, needs a calcium channel blocker that also slows the SA node. Which drug should Marielle get?
bank.why: Non-dihydropyridines (verapamil, diltiazem) also slow the heart; -dipines mainly dilate vessels.
bank.hint: V and D visit the heart.

dw.Amlodipine: A -dipine: it dilates vessels and barely touches the SA node.
dw.Nifedipine: A -dipine: it can even cause reflex tachycardia.
dw.Felodipine: A -dipine: mainly vessels, not the heart.

bank.q: Which calcium channel blocker is NOT a dihydropyridine?
bank.why: Non-DHP: verapamil, diltiazem.

dw.Nifedipine: Ends in -dipine, so it IS a dihydropyridine.
dw.Nicardipine: Ends in -dipine, so it IS a dihydropyridine.
dw.Felodipine: Ends in -dipine, so it IS a dihydropyridine.

bank.q: Verapamil, diltiazem and nifedipine share which mechanism in Table 11-3?
bank.why: They are the calcium channel blockers.

bank.q: Nitroprusside and fenoldopam are oral vasodilators.
bank.why: Nitroprusside and fenoldopam are parenteral; hydralazine and minoxidil are oral.

bank.q: Minoxidil lowers BP by releasing nitric oxide.
bank.why: Minoxidil opens K+ channels (hyperpolarization); hydralazine and nitroprusside release NO.

bank.q: The renin-angiotensin system is triggered by...
bank.a: A drop in blood pressure or fluid volume
d: A rise in blood pressure or fluid volume
High blood glucose after a meal
Excess sodium reaching the distal tubule
bank.why: Drop in BP or volume → kidney releases renin.

dw.A rise in blood pressure or fluid volume: Reversed: RAAS RAISES BP, so a drop triggers it.
dw.Excess sodium reaching the distal tubule: Plenty of sodium tells the kidney volume is fine, so renin goes DOWN.

bank.q: Renin is released by the...
bank.why: Renin from the kidney acts on angiotensinogen from the liver.

bank.q: Angiotensinogen is made by the...
bank.why: The liver makes angiotensinogen; renin cuts it to angiotensin I.

bank.q: Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) comes mainly from the...
bank.why: ACE (released from the lungs) turns angiotensin I into angiotensin II.
bank.hint: Where blood passes through all at once.

bank.q: Angiotensin II raises blood pressure by...
d: Dilating vessels and making the heart release ANP
Slowing the heart and lowering cardiac output
Increasing urine output and sodium loss
bank.why: Ang II → vasoconstriction + aldosterone (salt and water retention).

bank.q: Aldosterone acts on the kidneys to...
bank.why: More salt and water kept → more volume → higher BP.

dw.Release renin: Renin comes first in the cascade; aldosterone is at the end.

bank.q: Which drug blocks renin?
bank.why: R-A-A-A: Renin (aliskiren) → ACE (-pril) → AT1 receptor (-sartan) → Aldosterone (spironolactone, eplerenone).

bank.q: ACE is the same enzyme as...
bank.why: ACE (kininase II) also breaks down bradykinin. Kallikrein is the enzyme that makes bradykinin from kininogen.

dw.Renin: Renin cuts angiotensinogen; it's a different enzyme.
dw.Kallikrein: Kallikrein MAKES bradykinin; kininase II breaks it down.
dw.Carbonic anhydrase: That's acetazolamide's target in the PCT.

bank.q: Bradykinin lowers blood pressure by...
bank.a: Causing vasodilation and increasing prostaglandin synthesis
d: Releasing aldosterone from the adrenal cortex
Increasing heart rate and cardiac output
bank.why: Bradykinin → vasodilation (+ prostaglandins) → ↓ peripheral resistance.

dw.Causing vasoconstriction and blocking pr: Reversed: bradykinin DILATES and adds prostaglandins.

bank.q: Captopril lowers BP by...
bank.a: Inhibiting ACE: less angiotensin II, more bradykinin
d: Blocking AT1 receptors for angiotensin II
Blocking renin, the first step of the system
Blocking aldosterone receptors in the kidney
bank.why: ACE inhibitors lower Ang II AND raise bradykinin.

bank.q: Which drug is an ACE inhibitor?
bank.why: ACE inhibitors end in -pril: captopril, enalapril, ramipril. Losartan = ARB, aliskiren = renin inhibitor, amlodipine = CCB.

dw.Amlodipine: -dipine = CCB.

bank.q: Two weeks after starting a new antihypertensive, Lucille has a persistent dry, tickly cough. Which drug is responsible?
bank.why: ACE inhibitors → extra bradykinin → dry cough (and angioedema). ARBs don't affect bradykinin.

dw.Losartan: An ARB leaves bradykinin alone, so no cough.
dw.Amlodipine: CCB side effects are flushing, edema and headache, not cough.
dw.Hydrochlorothiazide: Thiazide toxicity is LUNA, not cough.

bank.q: Which drug gives Lucille the same angiotensin blockade WITHOUT the cough?
bank.why: ARBs block the AT1 receptor and leave bradykinin alone, so no cough.

dw.Amlodipine: No cough, but it's a CCB, not angiotensin blockade.
dw.Hydrochlorothiazide: A diuretic, not angiotensin blockade.

bank.q: An hour after his new BP pill, Christopher's lips and face swell up suddenly. Which drug most likely caused it?
bank.why: ACEi toxicity: dry cough, angioedema (the slide's swollen-lip photo), contraindicated in pregnancy.

dw.Amlodipine: CCBs cause ankle edema and flushing, not lip swelling.
dw.Furosemide: Loop toxicity is ototoxicity and allergy.
dw.Prazosin: Prazosin's classic problem is first-dose fainting (orthostatic hypotension).

bank.q: Which antihypertensive is contraindicated in pregnancy?
bank.why: ACE inhibitors (and ARBs) are contraindicated in pregnancy. Methyldopa and β-blockers can be used.
bank.hint: The E in ACE is for embryo.

bank.q: Elrin has type 2 diabetes, protein in her urine and hypertension. Which drug reduces proteinuria and stabilizes kidney function?
bank.why: Slide: ACE inhibitors are used in chronic kidney disease, especially in diabetics, because they diminish proteinuria.

dw.Amlodipine: It lowers BP but doesn't reduce proteinuria like an ACE inhibitor.
dw.Propranolol: A β-blocker; no kidney protection, and it can mask hypoglycemia in diabetics.

bank.q: ARBs such as valsartan lower BP by...
d: Blocking ACE, so less angiotensin II is made
Blocking renin, so less angiotensin I is made
Blocking ENaC in the collecting duct
bank.why: ARBs block AT1; more selective than ACE inhibitors.

bank.q: Which drug is an angiotensin receptor blocker?
bank.why: ARBs: losartan, valsartan, candesartan, irbesartan, telmisartan.

bank.q: ARBs differ from ACE inhibitors because they...
bank.why: Slide: more selective blockers of angiotensin effects than ACE inhibitors (no effect on bradykinin).

dw.Increase bradykinin more: Reversed: ARBs leave bradykinin alone. ACE inhibitors raise it.
dw.Are safe in pregnancy: ARBs are contraindicated in pregnancy, like ACE inhibitors.

bank.q: Which is NOT an effect of AT1 receptor stimulation?
bank.why: AT1: vasoconstriction, sympathetic activation, cell proliferation, aldosterone release, renal Na+ reabsorption. AT2: vasodilation, inhibition of cell growth, apoptosis.

dw.Vasoconstriction: It IS an AT1 effect, the main one.

bank.q: Stimulation of AT2 receptors causes...
bank.a: Vasodilation, inhibition of cell growth and apoptosis
bank.why: ARBs block AT1 and leave AT2 working.

bank.q: On the RAAS diagram, spironolactone and eplerenone block...
