bank.why: They act at the end of the cascade (aldosterone → Na+ and water retention).

bank.q: Which lists the RAAS blockers from the TOP of the cascade down?
bank.why: R-A-A-A: Renin, ACE, Angiotensin receptor, Aldosterone.

dw.Captopril → aliskiren → spironolactone →: Renin (aliskiren) is the top; the order is R-A-A-A.
dw.Losartan → captopril → aliskiren → spiro: Backwards for the first three. The top is renin (aliskiren).
dw.Spironolactone → losartan → captopril →: Fully reversed: that's bottom to top.

bank.q: ACE inhibitors and ARBs are both contraindicated in pregnancy.
bank.why: Both block the RAAS, which the fetal kidney needs.

bank.q: Losartan causes a dry cough by raising bradykinin.
bank.why: ARBs have no effect on bradykinin; the cough is an ACE inhibitor problem.

bank.q: In the treatment algorithm, management starts in adults with a BP of...
bank.why: Adults with BP ≥ 140/90 → advise therapeutic lifestyle changes.

dw.≥ 120/80 mmHg: 120/80 is already stage 1 by category, but the algorithm starts at 140/90.
dw.≥ 130/80 mmHg: That's the stage-1 threshold, not where the algorithm starts.
dw.≥ 180/120 mmHg: That's a crisis, far past where management starts.

bank.q: Which is NOT among the therapeutic lifestyle changes in the algorithm?
bank.why: Lifestyle: low-salt diet, weight loss, exercise, smoking cessation, alcohol abstinence.

dw.Weight loss: It IS a lifestyle change on the list.

bank.q: Mang Pedro has BP 150/95 and had a stroke last year (CV disease). What is the next step?
bank.a: Start a first-line drug along with lifestyle changes
d: Lifestyle changes alone for 3 months first
Refer him to a specialist right away
Start a β-blocker as the only drug
bank.why: With HMOD, CV disease or high risk → choose first-line drugs (monotherapy or combination) right away.

dw.Lifestyle changes alone for 3 months fir: Only for LOW-risk patients. A past stroke = CV disease, so start drugs now.
dw.Refer him to a specialist right away: Referral comes after failing the combination drugs.
dw.Start a β-blocker as the only drug: β-blockers aren't first line without a reason (e.g. CAD).

bank.q: Josh, 40, has BP 145/92 with no organ damage, no CV disease and low risk. What is the next step?
bank.a: Lifestyle changes, then recheck after 3 months
d: Start two drugs immediately at full doses
Refer him to a specialist this week
Start a β-blocker and recheck in a month
bank.why: Not high risk → lifestyle first; if targets aren't reached after 3 months, start first-line drugs.

dw.Start two drugs immediately at full dose: He's low risk, so lifestyle comes first.
dw.Refer him to a specialist this week: Referral is for when combination drugs fail.
dw.Start a β-blocker and recheck in a month: Low risk means lifestyle first, and β-blockers aren't first line anyway.

bank.q: Which drug is NOT among the first-line choices in the algorithm?
bank.why: First line: ACE inhibitor, ARB, CCB, thiazide (A-C-D). β-blockers wait for a reason.

dw.Amlodipine: A CCB: first line.
dw.Hydrochlorothiazide: A thiazide: first line.

bank.q: The first-line classes in the algorithm are...
bank.a: ACE inhibitors, ARBs, CCBs and thiazide diuretics
d: β-blockers, α-blockers, loop diuretics and vasodilators
ACE inhibitors, β-blockers, clonidine and minoxidil
Loop diuretics, ARBs, nitroprusside and aliskiren
bank.why: A-C-D: ACEi or ARB, CCB, Diuretic (thiazide).

dw.β-blockers, α-blockers, loop diuretics a: None of these are first line.
dw.ACE inhibitors, β-blockers, clonidine an: Only the ACE inhibitors are first line.
dw.Loop diuretics, ARBs, nitroprusside and: Only the ARBs are first line.

bank.q: Which is a PREFERRED combination in the algorithm?
bank.why: Preferred: ACEi/ARB + CCB and ACEi/ARB + HCTZ. An ACEi with an ARB doubles up on the same system; two K-sparing drugs risk hyperkalemia.
bank.hint: Mix A with C or D.

dw.Enalapril + losartan: ACEi + ARB block the same system twice, which is not preferred.
dw.Spironolactone + amiloride: Two K-sparing drugs together risk dangerous hyperkalemia.

bank.q: Which is also a preferred combination?
bank.why: ARB + HCTZ is preferred; the others double up on one class.

dw.Losartan + captopril: ARB + ACEi double up on the same system.
dw.Atenolol + metoprolol: Two β-blockers: the same class twice.
dw.Furosemide + bumetanide: Two loop diuretics: the same class twice.

bank.q: After 3 months on amlodipine alone, Samantha's BP is still above target. What does the algorithm say?
d: Stop amlodipine and give lifestyle advice only
bank.why: On monotherapy and not at target → add a 2nd agent from the first-line drugs.

dw.Stop amlodipine and give lifestyle advic: She's already above target ON a drug; stopping makes it worse.
dw.Refer her immediately: Referral comes after combination drugs fail.
dw.Switch to a β-blocker: β-blockers aren't first line. Add a 2nd first-line drug instead.

bank.q: Sharifah, on two first-line drugs, is still above target after 3 months. Next step?
bank.a: Add another drug from the first-line choices
d: Stop both drugs and start lifestyle changes
Keep the same drugs for another year
bank.why: Already on 2 drugs → add another first-line drug; if still not at target on the combination → refer.

dw.Stop both drugs and start lifestyle chan: Stopping drugs that are partly working makes BP worse.
dw.Keep the same drugs for another year: Not at target after 3 months means change now: add a 3rd first-line drug.

bank.q: When does the algorithm say to refer the patient?
bank.a: When BP targets aren't reached on the combination drugs
d: After the first month of lifestyle changes
bank.why: Not achieved on combination drugs → refer.

dw.As soon as BP is ≥ 140/90: At 140/90, management STARTS (lifestyle or drugs); it's not a referral.
dw.After the first month of lifestyle chang: Lifestyle gets 3 months, and then drugs come before referral.
dw.Only if the patient asks: Referral follows the algorithm: failing combination drugs.

bank.q: Resistant hypertension is BP that stays uncontrolled on...
bank.a: 3 drugs, one of which is a diuretic
bank.why: Footnote: uncontrolled on 3-drug combinations including a diuretic → refer for work-up or second-line agents.

dw.1 drug at full dose: One drug failing just means adding another.
dw.2 drugs of any class: It's 3 drugs, and one must be a diuretic.
dw.Lifestyle changes alone: Failing lifestyle just means starting drugs.

bank.q: In which patient may a β-blocker be the INITIAL antihypertensive?
bank.a: A patient with coronary artery disease
d: A young patient with no other disease
bank.why: β-blockers may be initial therapy with CAD, acute coronary syndrome, high sympathetic drive, or in pregnant women.

dw.A young patient with no other disease: No reason for a β-blocker, so start with A-C-D first line.
dw.A patient with gout: Gout is a reason to avoid thiazides, not to choose a β-blocker.

bank.q: Which drug is the WRONG choice for a pregnant woman with hypertension?
bank.why: ARBs and ACE inhibitors are contraindicated in pregnancy. Methyldopa and β-blockers (labetalol) are used.

dw.Methyldopa: Methyldopa IS the pregnancy drug ("para lang sa buntis").
dw.Labetalol: Labetalol is safe and used in pregnancy.

bank.q: Kyle, hypertensive and diabetic, takes glipizide and an antihypertensive. She is found confused, sweating and trembling. What is the problem, and which drug causes it?
bank.why: Confusion + sweating + trembling = hypoglycemia; glipizide (sulfonylurea) forces insulin release. Name the problem first, then the class.

dw.Hyperglycemia from glipizide: Glipizide LOWERS sugar (it releases insulin), and sweating and trembling mean LOW sugar.
dw.Hypotension from her antihypertensive: Low BP causes dizziness or fainting, not sweating and trembling.
dw.Hyperkalemia from glipizide: Sulfonylureas don't raise K+; the picture is hypoglycemia.

bank.q: Aleeyah has diabetes with proteinuria and BP 150/95. Which first-line drug also protects her kidneys?
bank.why: ACE inhibitors diminish proteinuria and stabilize renal function, especially in diabetics.

dw.Amlodipine: A first-line CCB, but it doesn't reduce proteinuria.
dw.Hydrochlorothiazide: First line, but no kidney protection (and it can raise blood sugar).
dw.Propranolol: Not first line, and it can mask hypoglycemia in diabetics.

bank.q: Marco, who is hypertensive, has had repeated gout attacks. Which first-line drug is the poorest choice for him?
bank.why: Thiazides raise uric acid (gout is in their toxicity list).

dw.Losartan: ARBs don't cause gout (losartan even lowers uric acid a little).
dw.Amlodipine: CCBs don't affect uric acid.

bank.q: Venice has asthma and needs BP control. Which drug should be AVOIDED?
bank.why: Propranolol is nonselective and blocks β2 in the lungs → bronchospasm.

dw.Amlodipine: CCBs don't touch β2, so they're safe in asthma.
dw.Hydrochlorothiazide: A thiazide: safe in asthma.

bank.q: Reine, on enalapril, is started on another drug and develops a dangerously high K+. Which drug was most likely added?
bank.why: ACE inhibitors lower aldosterone (keeping K+) and spironolactone blocks aldosterone: together they raise K+. Loops and thiazides lower K+.

dw.Furosemide: A loop wastes K+, so it would LOWER it.
dw.Hydrochlorothiazide: A thiazide LOWERS K+.
dw.Amlodipine: A CCB doesn't change K+.

bank.q: A patient took a large overdose of verapamil. Which antidote from Lesson 1 is used?
bank.why: Table 4-9: Ca2+ channel blockers → high-dose insulin and calcium.

dw.Glucagon only, as for β-blockers: Glucagon is the β-blocker antidote; CCBs need insulin and calcium.

bank.q: A patient took a large overdose of his propranolol. Which antidote?
bank.why: Table 4-9: glucagon for β-adrenergic antagonists.

dw.Calcium gluconate: Calcium (with high-dose insulin) is for CCB overdose.

bank.q: Match the ending: a drug ending in -sartan is a(n)...
bank.why: -pril = ACEi, -sartan = ARB, -dipine = CCB, -kiren = renin inhibitor, -olol = β-blocker, -zosin = α1 blocker.

bank.q: A drug ending in -pril is a(n)...
bank.why: -pril = ACE inhibitor (captopril, enalapril, ramipril).

bank.q: A drug ending in -dipine is a(n)...
bank.why: -dipine = DHP CCB (amlodipine, nifedipine…).

dw.Thiazide-like diuretic: Chlorthalidone, indapamide, metolazone: no shared ending.

bank.q: An ACE inhibitor plus an ARB is one of the preferred combinations.
bank.why: Preferred: ACEi/ARB + CCB, or ACEi/ARB + HCTZ. Combining an ACEi with an ARB doubles up on the same system.

bank.q: According to the algorithm notes, β-blockers may be used as initial therapy in pregnant women.
bank.why: Beta-blockers may be used as initial therapy with CAD, ACS, high sympathetic drive and in pregnant women.

bank.q: Kyle's repeated readings average 129/79 mmHg. What is the BP category?
bank.why: Systolic 120–129 AND diastolic < 80 = elevated. One more point on either number would make it stage 1.
bank.hint: Check BOTH numbers; the higher category wins.

dw.Normal: Normal needs BOTH below 120 AND below 80; a systolic of 129 is not below it.
dw.Hypertension stage 1: Stage 1 needs a systolic of 130–139 OR a diastolic of 80–89; 129/79 has neither.
dw.Hypertension stage 2: Stage 2 needs a systolic of 140 or more, OR a diastolic of 90 or more; 129/79 reaches neither.
dw.Hypertensive crisis: A crisis needs a systolic ABOVE 180 or a diastolic ABOVE 120; 129/79 has neither.

bank.q: Aaliya's repeated readings average 130/79 mmHg. What is the BP category?
bank.why: Systolic 130 is the first stage-1 number (130–139 OR 80–89).
bank.hint: Check BOTH numbers; the higher category wins.

dw.Normal: Normal needs BOTH below 120 AND below 80; a systolic of 130 is not below it.
dw.Elevated: Elevated stops at a systolic of 129; 130 is past it.
dw.Hypertension stage 2: Stage 2 needs a systolic of 140 or more, OR a diastolic of 90 or more; 130/79 reaches neither.
dw.Hypertensive crisis: A crisis needs a systolic ABOVE 180 or a diastolic ABOVE 120; 130/79 has neither.

bank.q: Josh's repeated readings average 120/80 mmHg. What is the BP category?
bank.why: Trap: 120 looks elevated, but a diastolic of 80 is already in the stage-1 range (80–89), and stage 1 needs only one number.
bank.hint: Check BOTH numbers; the higher category wins.

dw.Normal: Normal needs BOTH below 120 AND below 80; a systolic of 120 and a diastolic of 80 are not below them.
dw.Elevated: Elevated needs the diastolic BELOW 80 (it uses AND). A diastolic of 80 already counts as stage 1 (80–89).
dw.Hypertension stage 2: Stage 2 needs a systolic of 140 or more, OR a diastolic of 90 or more; 120/80 reaches neither.
dw.Hypertensive crisis: A crisis needs a systolic ABOVE 180 or a diastolic ABOVE 120; 120/80 has neither.

bank.q: Yuri's repeated readings average 139/89 mmHg. What is the BP category?
bank.why: Both numbers are at the top of stage 1 (139 and 89); neither reaches 140 or 90.
bank.hint: Check BOTH numbers; the higher category wins.

dw.Normal: Normal needs BOTH below 120 AND below 80; a systolic of 139 and a diastolic of 89 are not below them.
dw.Elevated: Elevated needs the diastolic BELOW 80 (it uses AND). A diastolic of 89 already counts as stage 1 (80–89).
dw.Hypertension stage 2: Stage 2 needs a systolic of 140 or more, OR a diastolic of 90 or more; 139/89 reaches neither.
dw.Hypertensive crisis: A crisis needs a systolic ABOVE 180 or a diastolic ABOVE 120; 139/89 has neither.

bank.q: Jeorlyn's repeated readings average 140/89 mmHg. What is the BP category?
bank.why: Systolic 140 = stage 2, even though the diastolic is only stage 1. The higher category wins.
bank.hint: Check BOTH numbers; the higher category wins.

dw.Normal: Normal needs BOTH below 120 AND below 80; a systolic of 140 and a diastolic of 89 are not below them.
dw.Elevated: Elevated needs the diastolic BELOW 80 (it uses AND). A diastolic of 89 already counts as stage 1 (80–89).
dw.Hypertension stage 1: Stage 1 is 130–139 OR 80–89, but the systolic 140 reaches stage 2, and the higher category wins.
dw.Hypertensive crisis: A crisis needs a systolic ABOVE 180 or a diastolic ABOVE 120; 140/89 has neither.

bank.q: Steve's repeated readings average 128/90 mmHg. What is the BP category?
bank.why: Diastolic 90 alone makes it stage 2 (≥140 OR ≥90).
bank.hint: Check BOTH numbers; the higher category wins.

dw.Normal: Normal needs BOTH below 120 AND below 80; a systolic of 128 and a diastolic of 90 are not below them.
dw.Elevated: Elevated needs the diastolic BELOW 80 (it uses AND). A diastolic of 90 already counts as stage 2 (≥ 90).
dw.Hypertension stage 1: Stage 1 is 130–139 OR 80–89, but the diastolic 90 reaches stage 2, and the higher category wins.
dw.Hypertensive crisis: A crisis needs a systolic ABOVE 180 or a diastolic ABOVE 120; 128/90 has neither.

bank.q: Sophia's repeated readings average 112/72 mmHg. What is the BP category?
bank.why: Below 120 AND below 80 = normal.
bank.hint: Check BOTH numbers; the higher category wins.

dw.Elevated: Elevated starts at a systolic of 120; 112 is still normal.
dw.Hypertension stage 1: Stage 1 needs a systolic of 130–139 OR a diastolic of 80–89; 112/72 has neither.
dw.Hypertension stage 2: Stage 2 needs a systolic of 140 or more, OR a diastolic of 90 or more; 112/72 reaches neither.
dw.Hypertensive crisis: A crisis needs a systolic ABOVE 180 or a diastolic ABOVE 120; 112/72 has neither.

bank.q: Harly's repeated readings average 182/100 mmHg. What is the BP category?
bank.why: Systolic above 180 = hypertensive crisis (above 180 and/or above 120).
bank.hint: Check BOTH numbers; the higher category wins.

dw.Normal: Normal needs BOTH below 120 AND below 80; a systolic of 182 and a diastolic of 100 are not below them.
dw.Elevated: Elevated needs the diastolic BELOW 80 (it uses AND). A diastolic of 100 already counts as stage 2 (≥ 90).
dw.Hypertension stage 1: Stage 1 is 130–139 OR 80–89, but the systolic 182 reaches hypertensive crisis, and the higher category wins.
dw.Hypertension stage 2: 182/100 goes ABOVE 180, which makes it a crisis, past stage 2.

bank.q: Christopher's repeated readings average 165/122 mmHg. What is the BP category?
bank.why: Diastolic above 120 = crisis, even with a systolic under 180 (and/or).
bank.hint: Check BOTH numbers; the higher category wins.

dw.Normal: Normal needs BOTH below 120 AND below 80; a systolic of 165 and a diastolic of 122 are not below them.
dw.Elevated: Elevated needs the diastolic BELOW 80 (it uses AND). A diastolic of 122 already counts as a crisis.
dw.Hypertension stage 1: Stage 1 is 130–139 OR 80–89, but the diastolic 122 reaches hypertensive crisis, and the higher category wins.
dw.Hypertension stage 2: 165/122 goes ABOVE 120, which makes it a crisis, past stage 2.

bank.q: Cas's repeated readings average 180/110 mmHg. What is the BP category?
bank.why: Crisis needs ABOVE 180 or ABOVE 120. Exactly 180/110 is still stage 2 (≥140 or ≥90).
bank.hint: Check BOTH numbers; the higher category wins.

dw.Normal: Normal needs BOTH below 120 AND below 80; a systolic of 180 and a diastolic of 110 are not below them.
dw.Elevated: Elevated needs the diastolic BELOW 80 (it uses AND). A diastolic of 110 already counts as stage 2 (≥ 90).
dw.Hypertension stage 1: Stage 1 is 130–139 OR 80–89, but the systolic 180 reaches stage 2, and the higher category wins.
dw.Hypertensive crisis: A crisis needs ABOVE 180 or ABOVE 120. 180/110 is AT the limit, not above it, so it stays stage 2.

bank.q: Gian's repeated readings average 126/84 mmHg. What is the BP category?
bank.why: Systolic 126 is elevated-range, but diastolic 84 is stage-1 range; stage 1 wins.
bank.hint: Check BOTH numbers; the higher category wins.

dw.Normal: Normal needs BOTH below 120 AND below 80; a systolic of 126 and a diastolic of 84 are not below them.
dw.Elevated: Elevated needs the diastolic BELOW 80 (it uses AND). A diastolic of 84 already counts as stage 1 (80–89).
dw.Hypertension stage 2: Stage 2 needs a systolic of 140 or more, OR a diastolic of 90 or more; 126/84 reaches neither.
dw.Hypertensive crisis: A crisis needs a systolic ABOVE 180 or a diastolic ABOVE 120; 126/84 has neither.

bank.q: Marti's repeated readings average 119/80 mmHg. What is the BP category?
bank.why: Normal needs a diastolic BELOW 80; 80 is stage 1 (80–89).
bank.hint: Check BOTH numbers; the higher category wins.

dw.Normal: Normal needs BOTH below 120 AND below 80; a diastolic of 80 is not below it.
dw.Elevated: Elevated needs the diastolic BELOW 80 (it uses AND). A diastolic of 80 already counts as stage 1 (80–89).
dw.Hypertension stage 2: Stage 2 needs a systolic of 140 or more, OR a diastolic of 90 or more; 119/80 reaches neither.
dw.Hypertensive crisis: A crisis needs a systolic ABOVE 180 or a diastolic ABOVE 120; 119/80 has neither.

bank.q: Venice's repeated readings average 135/95 mmHg. What is the BP category?
bank.why: Systolic 135 is stage 1, but diastolic 95 is stage 2; the higher category wins.
bank.hint: Check BOTH numbers; the higher category wins.

dw.Normal: Normal needs BOTH below 120 AND below 80; a systolic of 135 and a diastolic of 95 are not below them.
dw.Elevated: Elevated needs the diastolic BELOW 80 (it uses AND). A diastolic of 95 already counts as stage 2 (≥ 90).
dw.Hypertension stage 1: Stage 1 is 130–139 OR 80–89, but the diastolic 95 reaches stage 2, and the higher category wins.
dw.Hypertensive crisis: A crisis needs a systolic ABOVE 180 or a diastolic ABOVE 120; 135/95 has neither.

bank.q: Darryl's repeated readings average 124/76 mmHg. What is the BP category?
bank.why: Systolic 120–129 with diastolic below 80 = elevated.
bank.hint: Check BOTH numbers; the higher category wins.

dw.Normal: Normal needs BOTH below 120 AND below 80; a systolic of 124 is not below it.
dw.Hypertension stage 1: Stage 1 needs a systolic of 130–139 OR a diastolic of 80–89; 124/76 has neither.
dw.Hypertension stage 2: Stage 2 needs a systolic of 140 or more, OR a diastolic of 90 or more; 124/76 reaches neither.
dw.Hypertensive crisis: A crisis needs a systolic ABOVE 180 or a diastolic ABOVE 120; 124/76 has neither.

bank.q: Which reading is ELEVATED, not stage 1 hypertension?
bank.why: Elevated = 120–129 AND < 80. 132 is stage-1 systolic; 82 and 80 are stage-1 diastolics.

dw.132/78 mmHg: 132/78 mmHg is hypertension stage 1: the systolic 132 is in the stage-1 range (130–139 OR 80–89).
dw.118/82 mmHg: 118/82 mmHg is hypertension stage 1: the diastolic 82 is in the stage-1 range (130–139 OR 80–89).
dw.128/80 mmHg: 128/80 mmHg is hypertension stage 1: the diastolic 80 is in the stage-1 range (130–139 OR 80–89).

bank.q: Which reading is hypertension STAGE 2?
bank.why: ≥ 90 diastolic = stage 2 even with a stage-1 systolic.

dw.138/88 mmHg: 138/88 mmHg is hypertension stage 1: the systolic 138 is in the stage-1 range (130–139 OR 80–89).
dw.130/85 mmHg: 130/85 mmHg is hypertension stage 1: the systolic 130 is in the stage-1 range (130–139 OR 80–89).
dw.125/79 mmHg: 125/79 mmHg is elevated: systolic 120–129 with a diastolic below 80.

bank.q: Which reading is a HYPERTENSIVE CRISIS?
bank.why: Crisis = ABOVE 180 and/or ABOVE 120. 180/120 is exactly at the limits, so not above.

dw.178/118 mmHg: 178/118 mmHg is hypertension stage 2: the systolic 178 reaches stage 2 (≥ 140 OR ≥ 90). It never goes ABOVE 180 or 120, so it's not a crisis.
dw.160/100 mmHg: 160/100 mmHg is hypertension stage 2: the systolic 160 reaches stage 2 (≥ 140 OR ≥ 90). It never goes ABOVE 180 or 120, so it's not a crisis.
dw.180/120 mmHg: 180/120 mmHg is hypertension stage 2: 180 and 120 are the limits, and a crisis must go ABOVE them.

bank.q: The "Elevated" category is defined as...
bank.why: Elevated uses AND; it only raises the systolic.
bank.hint: Only the top number is up.

dw.Systolic 120–129 OR diastolic 80–89: Elevated uses AND, and a diastolic of 80–89 is already stage 1.

bank.q: Hypertension stage 1 is defined as...
bank.why: Stage 1 uses OR.

dw.Systolic 130–139 AND diastolic 80–89: Stage 1 uses OR: one number in range is enough.

bank.q: A hypertensive crisis is a BP...
bank.why: Crisis = > 180 and/or > 120.

dw.Above 160 and above 100: Those numbers are still stage 2. A crisis needs above 180 and/or above 120.
dw.Above 200 and above 130: Too high: it starts above 180 and/or above 120, and only one number is needed.

bank.q: One high reading in the clinic is enough to diagnose hypertension.
bank.why: Hypertension is based on repeated, reproducible measurements of elevated BP.

bank.q: A BP of 118/84 mmHg is hypertension stage 1.
bank.why: Diastolic 84 falls in 80–89; stage 1 needs only one number (OR).

bank.q: A nursing classmate tells Mara that 120/80 mmHg is a normal BP. According to the current guidelines discussed in class, 120/80 is...
bank.why: Dr. Orig's own example: normal is BELOW 120 and BELOW 80. A diastolic of 80 already satisfies stage 1 (80–89), and stage 1 uses OR.

dw.Normal: Normal needs BOTH below 120 AND below 80; a systolic of 120 and a diastolic of 80 are not below them.
dw.Elevated: Elevated needs the diastolic BELOW 80 (it uses AND). A diastolic of 80 already counts as stage 1 (80–89).
dw.Hypertension stage 2: Stage 2 needs a systolic of 140 or more, OR a diastolic of 90 or more; 120/80 reaches neither.

bank.q: Doc Tina's BP of 125/78 is elevated. If it were 125/80 instead, what would it be?
bank.why: Lecture example: 125/80 satisfies one stage-1 criterion (diastolic 80–89), so it's stage 1.

dw.Still elevated: Elevated needs a diastolic BELOW 80. At 80, the diastolic is in the stage-1 range.
dw.Normal: Normal needs below 120 AND below 80; 125/80 fails both.

bank.q: Ron's BP is 130/100 mmHg: the systolic is in the stage-1 range and the diastolic in the stage-2 range. What is his category?
bank.why: Answered in class: whichever number reaches the higher level takes precedence, so 130/100 is stage 2.

dw.Hypertension stage 1: Stage 1 is 130–139 OR 80–89, but the diastolic 100 reaches stage 2, and the higher category wins.
dw.Elevated: Elevated needs the diastolic BELOW 80 (it uses AND). A diastolic of 100 already counts as stage 2 (≥ 90).
dw.Hypertensive crisis: A crisis needs a systolic ABOVE 180 or a diastolic ABOVE 120; 130/100 has neither.

bank.q: Which condition discussed in class causes SECONDARY hypertension through high sympathetic stimulation?
bank.why: Dr. Orig corrected the class: not diabetes. Pheochromocytoma raises sympathetic stimulation; secondary hypertension has a specific etiology.

dw.Diabetes mellitus: He corrected the class on this: diabetes isn't the cause he meant. Pheochromocytoma is.
dw.Essential hypertension: Essential (primary) hypertension has NO known cause; it isn't secondary.
dw.Asthma: Asthma doesn't cause hypertension. Its link to BP drugs is that propranolol must be avoided.

bank.q: Most patients with hypertension have...
bank.a: Primary (essential) hypertension, with no known cause
bank.why: Lecture: most hypertensive patients have essential hypertension; the cause isn't known.

dw.Secondary hypertension from kidney disea: Secondary causes exist, but they're the minority.
dw.Secondary hypertension from pheochromocy: Pheochromocytoma is a rare secondary cause.
dw.Hypertensive crisis: A crisis is a dangerous level that few patients reach; it isn't the usual kind.

bank.q: Diuretics lower blood volume because...
d: They pull water into the cells
bank.why: Lecture: excreting sodium makes water follow into the urine → lower blood volume → lower BP.

dw.They pull water into the cells: Water leaves with the sodium in the urine; it doesn't go into cells.
dw.They block water channels directly: They block SODIUM transporters; water follows the sodium.
dw.They increase thirst: Thirst would add volume, the opposite of what they do.

bank.q: Which three diuretic classes did Dr. Orig say are used for hypertension?
d: Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, osmotic and loop
Loop, osmotic and carbonic anhydrase inhibitors
bank.why: He discussed loop (loop of Henle), thiazide (DCT) and K-sparing (collecting duct).

dw.Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, osmotic a: Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors and osmotic diuretics aren't used for BP.
dw.Osmotic, thiazide and potassium-sparing: Osmotic diuretics (mannitol) aren't used for BP.
dw.Loop, osmotic and carbonic anhydrase inh: Osmotic diuretics and carbonic anhydrase inhibitors aren't used for BP.

bank.q: What is the order of the nephron's parts?
bank.a: Glomerulus → PCT → loop of Henle → DCT → collecting duct
d: PCT → glomerulus → DCT → loop of Henle → collecting duct
Glomerulus → loop of Henle → PCT → collecting duct → DCT
Collecting duct → DCT → loop of Henle → PCT → glomerulus
bank.why: Glomerulus filters → proximal convoluted tubule → loop of Henle (descending, ascending) → distal convoluted tubule → collecting duct.

dw.PCT → glomerulus → DCT → loop of Henle →: The filter (glomerulus) comes first, and the loop comes before the DCT.
dw.Glomerulus → loop of Henle → PCT → colle: The PCT comes before the loop, and the DCT before the collecting duct.
dw.Collecting duct → DCT → loop of Henle →: Reversed: the filtrate starts at the glomerulus.

bank.q: "Push Lasix!" in medical dramas means giving IV...
bank.why: Lasix is the brand of furosemide, the most commonly used loop diuretic.

dw.Hydrochlorothiazide: HCTZ is an oral thiazide for hypertension, not the emergency IV drug.
dw.Spironolactone: Spironolactone's brand is Aldactone, and it's a weak oral K-sparing drug.
dw.Losartan: An ARB, not a diuretic (brand Cozaar).

bank.q: Which loop diuretic is the MOST potent?
bank.why: Asked in class: bumetanide needs the smallest dose (0.5–2 mg). Ethacrynic acid is the least potent; furosemide is the most commonly used.

dw.Furosemide: Furosemide is the most COMMONLY used, not the most potent.
dw.Torsemide: Torsemide needs more mg than bumetanide.
dw.Ethacrynic acid: Ethacrynic acid is the LEAST potent (largest dose).

bank.q: Which loop diuretic is the LEAST potent?
bank.why: It needs the largest dose (50–200 mg).

dw.Torsemide: Torsemide needs a smaller dose than ethacrynic acid, so it's more potent.

bank.q: Which loop diuretic is the most commonly used?
bank.why: Lecture: furosemide (Lasix) is the most common, even though bumetanide is more potent.

dw.Bumetanide: Bumetanide is the most POTENT, not the most used.
dw.Ethacrynic acid: Ethacrynic acid is the least potent and the least used.
dw.Torsemide: Torsemide is used less than furosemide.

bank.term: Odd one out of the loops
bank.q: None of these end in -ide. Which one is still a LOOP diuretic?
bank.why: "Memorize the four loop diuretics": furosemide, bumetanide and torsemide end in -ide; ethacrynic acid is the odd one.

dw.Spironolactone: Spironolactone is potassium-sparing (an aldosterone antagonist), not a loop.
dw.Triamterene: Triamterene is potassium-sparing (blocks ENaC), not a loop.
dw.Chlorthalidone: Chlorthalidone is a thiazide-like diuretic (blocks NCC in the DCT), not a loop.

bank.term: Heart failure patient who can't breathe
bank.q: Lola Nena, 65, had a heart attack and now arrives gasping, "Doc, I can't breathe!" Her lungs are full of fluid. What should be given?
bank.why: Dr. Orig's patient story: acute pulmonary edema from heart failure; IV furosemide made her urinate the fluid out and breathe within minutes.

dw.Oral hydrochlorothiazide: Too weak and too slow; she needs an IV loop now.
dw.Oral amlodipine: A CCB lowers BP but doesn't pull fluid out of the lungs.
dw.Spironolactone tablets: A weak oral K-sparing drug; too slow for an emergency.

bank.q: What is the NUMBER ONE use of loop diuretics?
bank.why: Uses: pulmonary edema (number one), hyperkalemia, acute renal failure (volume overload).

dw.Hypertension: Loops are TOO strong for routine BP; thiazides are used instead.
dw.Gout: Diuretics CAUSE gout (thiazides); they don't treat it.

bank.q: Why are loop diuretics usually NOT used for hypertension anymore?
bank.a: Their effect is too strong for routine BP control
bank.why: Lecture: they're too strong for routine BP control; thiazides are used instead.

dw.They raise blood pressure: They lower BP; they're just too strong as diuretics.
dw.They only work in pregnancy: No. The pregnancy BP drug is methyldopa.

bank.q: Which diuretic is the one commonly used for hypertension?
bank.why: Thiazides are weaker than loops, so they're the usual diuretic for hypertension; loops are preferred in heart failure.

dw.Furosemide: A loop: too strong for routine BP, and kept for edema.
dw.Bumetanide: A loop: too strong for routine BP.
dw.Ethacrynic acid: A loop: too strong for routine BP.

bank.q: Thiazides are weaker diuretics than loop diuretics because the transporter they block...
bank.a: Carries only Na+ and Cl− (no K+)
bank.why: NCC (Na+/Cl−) vs NKCC2 (Na+/K+/2Cl−).

dw.Is in the collecting duct: NCC is in the DCT; the collecting duct is the K-sparing drugs' site.
dw.Carries water only: NCC carries Na+ and Cl−, not water.
dw.Is blocked irreversibly: Irreversible blocking would make them stronger, not weaker.

bank.q: Thiazides cause gout because they...
bank.why: Lecture: more uric acid is reabsorbed → urate crystals in the joints → gout.

dw.Block uric acid production: Blocking production would PREVENT gout (that's allopurinol).
dw.Lower blood volume only: The key is that the kidney keeps more uric acid.
dw.Increase potassium: Thiazides LOWER potassium, and K+ doesn't cause gout anyway.

bank.q: Aldosterone is a hormone from the...
bank.why: Aldosterone comes from the adrenal cortex (angiotensin II stimulates it).

dw.Adrenal medulla: The medulla makes epinephrine and norepinephrine.
dw.Kidney: The kidney makes renin, which starts the cascade; aldosterone is made at its end, in the adrenal cortex.

bank.q: Aldosterone acts on the distal tubule and collecting duct to...
bank.why: Blocking it leaves sodium in the urine and potassium in the blood: that's why these diuretics are potassium-SPARING.

dw.Excrete sodium and reabsorb potassium: Reversed: aldosterone KEEPS sodium and gets rid of potassium.
dw.Excrete both sodium and potassium: Aldosterone keeps sodium (and water) to raise BP.
dw.Reabsorb glucose: Glucose is reabsorbed in the PCT (SGLT2), not by aldosterone.

bank.q: Aldosterone increases sodium reabsorption partly by upregulating...
bank.why: Lecture: aldosterone upregulates ENaC; amiloride and triamterene block ENaC directly.

dw.NKCC2 (Na-K-2Cl cotransporter): NKCC2 is in the TAL and is the loop diuretics' target.
dw.NCC (Na-Cl cotransporter): NCC is in the DCT and is the thiazides' target.
dw.SGLT2 (sodium-glucose cotransporter 2): SGLT2 reabsorbs glucose in the PCT (the -gliflozins' target).

bank.q: Which pair are aldosterone antagonists?
bank.why: Aldoster-ONE antagonists: spironolact-ONE, epleren-ONE. Amiloride and triamterene are the ENaC inhibitors.

dw.Amiloride and triamterene: Also K-sparing, but they block ENaC, not aldosterone.

bank.q: Which drug did Dr. Orig single out for causing gynecomastia (breast enlargement in men)?
bank.why: Spironolactone's peculiar toxicity is gynecomastia; all K-sparing diuretics can cause hyperkalemia.

dw.Eplerenone: Eplerenone is the more selective aldosterone blocker, made to AVOID gynecomastia.

bank.q: Loop diuretics are part of the management of drowning.
bank.why: Asked in class: not used for drowning. In pulmonary edema the fluid comes from the blood vessels; inhaled water doesn't.

bank.q: Potassium-sparing diuretics can also be used for hypertension.
bank.why: Lecture: uses are aldosteronism, heart failure, and even hypertension.

bank.q: Methyldopa and clonidine are...
bank.why: Dr. Orig caught the class saying "blockers": they are α2 AGONISTS (the presynaptic brake).

dw.α2 blockers: Blocking α2 would REMOVE the brake. They are AGONISTS (he caught the class on this).

bank.q: Of the sympatholytics, which are commonly given for hypertension?
bank.why: Lecture: commonly clonidine and β-blockers; methyldopa is only for pregnant patients.

dw.Methyldopa and phentolamine: Methyldopa is only for pregnancy; phentolamine is for pheochromocytoma.
dw.Phenoxybenzamine and prazosin: Phenoxybenzamine is for pheochromocytoma, not routine BP.
dw.Methyldopa for every patient: Methyldopa is kept for PREGNANT patients.

bank.q: Which sympatholytic did Dr. Orig say is only for pregnant patients?
bank.why: "Ang methyldopa, para lang siya sa mga buntis."

dw.Clonidine: Clonidine is commonly used in general, not only in pregnancy.
dw.Prazosin: An α1 blocker; not a pregnancy drug.
dw.Atenolol: A β1 blocker; the pregnancy β-blocker would be labetalol.

bank.q: Prazosin lowers BP because blocking α1 receptors...
bank.why: α1 = vasoconstriction; blocking it relaxes the vessels.

dw.Blocks renin release: Renin release is β1-driven; prazosin acts on α1 in the vessels.

bank.q: Which direct vasodilator is the most widely used today, though no longer for hypertension?
bank.why: Lecture: minoxidil is now applied to the scalp for hair loss; taken orally it has many side effects.

dw.Hydralazine: Still an oral BP drug (e.g. in pregnancy), but not the most used vasodilator today.

bank.q: Calcium entering vascular smooth muscle and heart cells...
bank.a: Causes vasoconstriction and increases heart rate
d: Causes vasodilation and slows the heart
bank.why: Lecture: "C for contraction": Ca2+ constricts vessels and speeds the heart, which is what CCBs block.

dw.Causes vasodilation and slows the heart: Reversed. "C for contraction": Ca2+ squeezes vessels and speeds the heart.
dw.Only affects skeletal muscle: Ca2+ drives smooth and cardiac muscle too, which is why CCBs work.

bank.q: Which calcium channel blocker is the most commonly used for hypertension?
bank.why: Lecture: dihydropyridines are mostly used, especially amlodipine (the most readily available).

dw.Verapamil: A non-DHP, used more for heart rate than for BP.
dw.Diltiazem: A non-DHP, used more for heart rate.
dw.Nicardipine: A DHP, but mostly IV; amlodipine is the common one.

bank.q: The two non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers are...
bank.why: Only two non-DHPs; the rest are -dipines.

dw.Amlodipine and nifedipine: Both end in -dipine, so they ARE dihydropyridines.
dw.Felodipine and nicardipine: Both end in -dipine, so they ARE dihydropyridines.

bank.q: The overall effect of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system is to...
bank.why: Lecture: every step of the RAAS raises BP, so to lower BP you block one of its steps.
bank.hint: It's activated when BP is low.

dw.Decrease blood pressure: Every RAAS step RAISES BP; that's why the drugs block a step.
dw.Lower blood volume: Aldosterone KEEPS salt and water, so volume goes UP.
dw.Lower heart rate: RAAS works on vessels and volume, and it raises BP.

bank.q: "Angio-tensin" means...
bank.why: Angio = blood vessel, tensin = tension: angiotensin II constricts the vessels.

dw.Blood clotting: Angio = vessel, tensin = tension. Nothing about clotting.
dw.Heart contraction: It's about the VESSELS (angio), not the heart.
dw.Kidney filtration: Angio = vessel; the name is about vessel tension.

bank.q: Angiotensin II stimulates which gland to secrete aldosterone?
bank.why: Ang II → adrenal cortex → aldosterone → Na+ reabsorption → more volume.

dw.Adrenal medulla: The medulla makes epinephrine and norepinephrine.

bank.q: "Alis ka, renin!" Aliskiren is a...
bank.why: Aliskiren blocks renin at the top of the cascade.

bank.q: Which drugs discussed earlier ALREADY block the aldosterone step of the RAAS?
d: Calcium channel blockers such as amlodipine
bank.why: Lecture: we already blocked aldosterone using the K-sparing diuretics.

dw.Loop diuretics such as furosemide: Loops block NKCC2 in the loop, not aldosterone.
dw.Thiazides such as HCTZ: Thiazides block NCC in the DCT, not aldosterone.
dw.Calcium channel blockers such as amlodip: CCBs aren't part of the RAAS at all.

bank.q: Ashlea's BP went up from stress, so she was prescribed captopril. A month later she complains of a constant dry cough. What should be done?
bank.a: Stop the ACE inhibitor and shift to an ARB
d: Add a cough syrup and continue captopril
Shift to another ACE inhibitor such as enalapril
bank.why: His "usual question": ACE inhibitors cause dry cough (and angioedema); ARBs don't, so switch to an -sartan.
bank.hint: Change the class, not the dose.

dw.Add a cough syrup and continue captopril: The cough comes from bradykinin and won't stop while she's on an ACE inhibitor.
dw.Double the captopril dose: More ACE inhibitor means more bradykinin and more cough.
dw.Shift to another ACE inhibitor such as e: Every -pril raises bradykinin, so the cough stays.

bank.q: Louisse got a dry cough on captopril. Which drug would replace it?
bank.why: Team Losartan: an ARB blocks the AT1 receptor without the ACE inhibitor's cough.

dw.Captopril at a lower dose: Still an ACE inhibitor, so the cough can continue.

bank.q: ARBs block the AT1 receptor, which is responsible mainly for...
bank.why: Lecture: the AT1 receptor mediates vasoconstriction; blocking it stops the squeeze.

dw.Vasodilation: Vasodilation is the AT2 (and bradykinin) effect.
dw.Bradycardia: AT1 stimulation doesn't slow the heart.
dw.Diuresis: AT1 does the opposite: it keeps sodium (through aldosterone).

bank.q: Many patients on captopril come back saying "Doc, why do I keep coughing?" The cough is a side effect of...
bank.why: Dry cough and angioedema are the common ACE inhibitor side effects.

dw.ARBs: ARBs leave bradykinin alone, so they're the switch FOR the cough.
dw.Calcium channel blockers: CCBs cause edema and flushing, not cough.
dw.Thiazide diuretics: Thiazide toxicity is LUNA, not cough.

bank.q: Dr. Orig said drugs are usually started when BP is...
d: Whenever the patient asks for drugs
bank.why: Lecture: not all hypertensives get drugs right away; ≥140/90 usually gets drugs, lower readings get lifestyle changes.

dw.≥ 120/80 mmHg, in every adult: Lower readings get lifestyle changes first.
dw.Only during a hypertensive crisis: Drugs start well before a crisis, from 140/90.
dw.Whenever the patient asks for drugs: The decision follows the BP and the risk, not the request.

bank.q: Rica has been on captopril for 3 months and her BP is still high. Which drug is usually added?
bank.why: Not at target on monotherapy → add another first-line drug; he added a CCB.

dw.Furosemide (a loop diuretic): Loops are too strong for routine BP.
dw.A second ACE inhibitor: Two drugs of the same class add nothing; add a different first-line class.

bank.q: After an ACE-inhibitor cough and a CCB add-on, Christelle ends up on the usual combination given to patients. Which is it?
bank.why: An ARB + a CCB: "amlodipine, then losartan", the usual combination.

dw.Captopril + losartan: ACEi + ARB double up on the same system, and she already had the ACEi cough.
dw.Furosemide + spironolactone: That's a heart-failure (edema) combination, not the usual BP pair.
dw.Methyldopa + clonidine: Two central α2 agonists, and methyldopa is for pregnancy.

bank.q: Once a patient's BP has been controlled for months or years, the doctor may...
bank.a: Slowly lower the doses or the number of drugs
d: Stop all the drugs at once, since BP is normal
Add a fourth drug to keep BP low
Switch every drug to a loop diuretic
bank.why: Lecture: stay on the regimen, then try to reduce the drugs or doses while keeping BP normal.

dw.Stop all the drugs at once, since BP is: BP is normal BECAUSE of the drugs; stopping suddenly makes it rebound.
dw.Add a fourth drug to keep BP low: A controlled BP doesn't need more drugs.
dw.Switch every drug to a loop diuretic: Loops are too strong for routine BP.

bank.q: A 30-year-old on ramipril for hypertension learns she is 8 weeks pregnant. What should be done?
bank.a: Stop ramipril and switch to methyldopa
d: Keep ramipril; it is safe after the first trimester
bank.why: ACE inhibitors and ARBs are contraindicated in pregnancy. Methyldopa (central α2 agonist) is Dr. Orig's pregnancy drug.

dw.Keep ramipril; it is safe after the firs: ACE inhibitors are contraindicated in the whole pregnancy.
dw.Switch ramipril to losartan: ARBs are contraindicated in pregnancy too.
dw.Add hydrochlorothiazide to ramipril: Adding a drug keeps the fetus exposed to the ACE inhibitor.

bank.q: Which patient should NOT be given losartan?
bank.a: A woman who is 20 weeks pregnant
d: A man with an ACE-inhibitor cough
A diabetic with protein in the urine
A man on amlodipine with stage 2 BP
bank.why: ARBs (and ACE inhibitors) are contraindicated in pregnancy.

dw.A man with an ACE-inhibitor cough: That's exactly who gets an ARB.
dw.A diabetic with protein in the urine: ARBs, like ACE inhibitors, protect the diabetic kidney.
dw.A man on amlodipine with stage 2 BP: ARB + CCB is a preferred combination.

bank.q: Two weeks after starting enalapril, Venice wakes up with swollen lips and tongue. What explains it?
d: An allergy to the sulfa group
bank.why: ACE is also kininase II. Blocking it raises bradykinin, which causes the cough and the angioedema.

dw.Too much angiotensin II: An ACE inhibitor LOWERS angiotensin II.
dw.An allergy to the sulfa group: Sulfa allergy belongs to loops and thiazides, not enalapril.

bank.q: Tracy's BP is controlled on captopril, but a dry cough won't go away. Which replacement keeps the RAAS blocked without the cough?
bank.why: Switch the ACE inhibitor to an ARB (-sartan): it blocks the AT1 receptor and leaves bradykinin alone.

dw.Enalapril: Another ACE inhibitor: same bradykinin, same cough.
dw.Amlodipine: A CCB; it lowers BP but doesn't block the RAAS.
dw.Propranolol: A β-blocker; not first line and doesn't block the RAAS.

bank.q: Aaliya has diabetes, hypertension and protein in the urine. Enalapril protected the kidneys but caused a dry cough. What is the best switch?
bank.why: Keep the RAAS blocked for the kidneys, but without bradykinin: an ARB.

dw.Captopril: Another ACE inhibitor: the cough stays.
dw.Amlodipine: Lowers BP but loses the RAAS kidney protection.
dw.Hydrochlorothiazide: Lowers BP but loses the RAAS kidney protection.

bank.q: Lucille's new drug lowers angiotensin II and raises bradykinin levels. Which drug is it?
bank.why: Only ACE inhibitors (-pril) block ACE = kininase II, so Ang II falls and bradykinin rises.

dw.Telmisartan: An ARB: blocks the AT1 receptor; bradykinin is unchanged.
dw.Spironolactone: Blocks aldosterone; angiotensin II is unchanged.

bank.q: Theresa's new drug blocks renin, the very first step of the RAAS. Which drug is it?
bank.why: R-A-A-A: Renin (aliskiren) → ACE (-pril) → Ang II receptor (-sartan) → Aldosterone (spironolactone, eplerenone).

dw.Losartan: Blocks the angiotensin II receptor (third step).

bank.term: High K+ after an added drug
bank.q: Reine takes enalapril. A diuretic is added for heart failure, and a week later Reine's K+ is 6.1 mEq/L. Which drug was most likely added?
bank.why: K-sparing diuretics cause hyperkalemia; with an ACE inhibitor (less aldosterone) the K+ climbs even more.

dw.Furosemide: Loops throw K+ out (they even treat hyperkalemia).
dw.Hydrochlorothiazide: Thiazides lower K+, not raise it.
dw.Amlodipine: A CCB, not a diuretic; it doesn't change K+.

bank.q: Princess has acute renal failure with fluid overload and a K+ of 6.4 mEq/L. Which diuretic helps both problems?
bank.why: Loop uses: pulmonary edema, hyperkalemia, acute renal failure. Loops pull out water and K+.

dw.Spironolactone: K-sparing: would push K+ even higher.
dw.Amiloride: K-sparing (ENaC blocker): would push K+ even higher.
dw.Methyldopa: A central α2 agonist, not a diuretic.

bank.q: Mara takes furosemide daily for heart failure and now has muscle cramps and a K+ of 2.9 mEq/L. Which diuretic can be added to correct the K+?
bank.why: A K-sparing diuretic holds on to K+ and is also used in heart failure.

dw.Hydrochlorothiazide: Thiazides also waste K+.

bank.q: Elrin's K+ is already 5.8 mEq/L and she needs a diuretic for her blood pressure. Which should be AVOIDED?
bank.why: K-sparing diuretics cause hyperkalemia; avoid them when K+ is already high.

dw.Hydrochlorothiazide: Lowers K+, so it is safe here.
dw.Furosemide: Lowers K+, so it is safe here.
dw.Chlorthalidone: Thiazide-like; lowers K+, so it is safe here.

bank.q: Ashlea has hypertension, low K+ and very high aldosterone from an adrenal tumor. Which diuretic targets the cause?
bank.why: Aldosterone antagonists (spironolactone, eplerenone) are used for hyperaldosteronism.

dw.Furosemide: A loop: would lower K+ even more.
dw.Hydrochlorothiazide: A thiazide: would lower K+ even more.
dw.Amlodipine: A CCB, not a diuretic; aldosterone is untouched.

bank.q: A 60-year-old man on spironolactone for heart failure develops painful breast enlargement. Which replacement works the same way with less of this effect?
bank.why: Eplerenone is the more selective aldosterone antagonist, so less gynecomastia.

dw.Amiloride: K-sparing too, but it blocks ENaC, a different mechanism.
dw.Furosemide: A loop: a different mechanism altogether.
dw.Losartan: An ARB: doesn't block the aldosterone receptor.

bank.q: Janah's BP is at target on hydrochlorothiazide, but gout has started. Which is the best switch to another first-line drug?
bank.why: Thiazide toxicity = LUNA (lipids up, uric acid up, Na+ down, allergy). First line = ACEi/ARB, CCB, thiazide.

dw.Prazosin: An α1 blocker; not a first-line drug.
dw.Clonidine: A central α2 agonist; not a first-line drug.

bank.q: Carylle takes amlodipine and one other antihypertensive. Labs show low sodium, high uric acid and high cholesterol. Which is the other drug?
bank.why: LUNA: Lipids up, Uric acid up, Na+ down, Allergy. That's a thiazide.

dw.Spironolactone: Its problem is high K+ (and gynecomastia).
dw.Clonidine: A central α2 agonist; not this pattern.

bank.q: Sharifah's hydrochlorothiazide blocks the Na+/Cl− cotransporter. In which part of the nephron?
bank.why: A-O-L-T-K down the nephron: acetazolamide (PCT), osmotic, loop (TAL), thiazide (DCT), K-sparing (collecting duct).
bank.hint: T for thiazide, D for distal.

bank.q: Marti, 35 and otherwise healthy, has BP averaging 145/92 on repeated visits. What is the best first step?
bank.a: Lifestyle changes for 3 months, then recheck
d: Refer to a specialist right away
bank.why: ≥140/90 and NOT high risk → lifestyle for 3 months; start drugs only if the target isn't reached.

dw.Start amlodipine and losartan today: Low-risk patients start with lifestyle changes first.
dw.Start propranolol today: β-blockers aren't initial therapy without a reason.

bank.q: Josh has diabetes with kidney damage (HMOD) and BP averaging 150/95. What should be done?
bank.a: Start drugs now, with lifestyle changes
d: Refer to a specialist right away
bank.why: High risk (HMOD, CV disease or equivalent) → start drugs now, together with lifestyle changes.

dw.Lifestyle changes alone for 3 months: That's only for patients who are NOT high risk.

bank.q: After 3 months on losartan alone, Steve's BP is still 146/94. What is the next step?
bank.why: Monotherapy not at target → add a 2nd first-line drug. ARB + CCB is a preferred combination.

dw.Add enalapril: Never combine an ACE inhibitor with an ARB.
dw.Switch to propranolol: β-blockers aren't first line without a reason.

bank.q: Jeorlyn takes amlodipine, losartan and hydrochlorothiazide at full doses, yet BP stays at 150/95. What is this, and what is done?
bank.a: Resistant hypertension; refer to a specialist
bank.why: Uncontrolled on 3 drugs, one of them a diuretic = resistant hypertension → specialist work-up or second-line agents.

dw.Hypertensive crisis; give IV nitroprussi: A crisis is above 180 and/or above 120.
dw.Resistant hypertension; add enalapril: Never add an ACE inhibitor to an ARB.
dw.Secondary hypertension; stop all drugs: Stopping all drugs would let BP climb.

bank.q: Christopher's prescription lists losartan, enalapril and amlodipine. What should be changed?
bank.a: Drop either the ACE inhibitor or the ARB
d: Drop amlodipine; CCBs don't mix with ARBs
Keep all three, but halve the enalapril
Nothing; this is a preferred combination
bank.why: Never combine an ACE inhibitor with an ARB (both are "A"). Preferred: ACEi/ARB + CCB or ACEi/ARB + HCTZ.

dw.Drop amlodipine; CCBs don't mix with ARB: ARB + CCB is a preferred combination.
dw.Keep all three, but halve the enalapril: A lower dose doesn't make ACEi + ARB acceptable.

bank.q: Cass is on enalapril and needs a second first-line drug. Which pair is a PREFERRED combination?
bank.why: Preferred combinations: ACEi/ARB + CCB and ACEi/ARB + HCTZ.

dw.Enalapril + spironolactone: Not a preferred pair; high K+ risk.
dw.Enalapril + propranolol: β-blockers aren't first line without a reason.

bank.q: Which patient may start on a β-blocker as the INITIAL drug?
bank.a: Sophia, with angina from coronary artery disease
d: Josef, with gout from a thiazide
bank.why: β-blockers as initial therapy only with CAD, acute coronary syndrome, high sympathetic drive or pregnancy.

dw.Darryl, 40, with no other illness: First line is ACEi/ARB, CCB or thiazide.
dw.Justyn, with diabetes and proteinuria: An ACEi or ARB protects the kidneys.

bank.q: Yuri arrives with BP 200/130, a severe headache and blurred vision. Which drug is given IV?
bank.why: A crisis (above 180 and/or above 120) needs a parenteral vasodilator: nitroprusside or fenoldopam.

dw.Methyldopa: An oral α2 agonist for pregnancy.

bank.q: In the ICU, Rica is given an IV antihypertensive that activates dopamine receptors. Which drug is it?
bank.why: Fenol-DOPA-m works on DOPAmine receptors.

dw.Nitroprusside: IV too, but it releases nitric oxide.

bank.q: Marco's oral antihypertensive opens K+ channels in arteries, and new hair is growing on the face and arms. Which drug?
bank.why: Minoxidil and diazoxide open K+ channels; minoxidil's hair growth became the topical hair-regrowth product.

dw.Hydralazine: Oral, but it releases nitric oxide.

bank.q: Gian takes verapamil, and the resting heart rate is now 48. What explains it?
bank.why: Non-dihydropyridines (verapamil, diltiazem) also slow the SA node; the -dipines act mainly on vessels.
bank.hint: V and D visit the heart.

dw.It blocks α1 receptors: That's prazosin (vessels, not the SA node).

bank.q: A 40-year-old has spikes of BP up to 210/120 with headache, sweating and palpitations from an adrenal medulla tumor. Which pair is used?
bank.why: PHEochromocytoma → PHEntolamine and PHEnoxybenzamine (α blockers).

dw.Methyldopa and clonidine: Central α2 agonists; they don't block the tumor's catecholamines at α1.
dw.Captopril and losartan: RAAS blockers; the problem here is catecholamines.
dw.Verapamil and diltiazem: CCBs; the problem here is catecholamines.

bank.q: A 65-year-old man has hypertension and a weak urine stream from an enlarged prostate. Which antihypertensive helps both?
bank.why: α1 blockers (-zosin) relax vascular AND prostate smooth muscle (Lesson 4).

dw.Hydrochlorothiazide: More urine, but it doesn't relax the prostate.
dw.Clonidine: A central α2 agonist; doesn't relax the prostate.
dw.Amlodipine: A CCB; doesn't relax the prostate.

bank.q: Gabriel has asthma and hypertension. Which drug should be AVOIDED?
bank.why: Nonselective β-blockers also block β2 in the lungs and can trigger bronchospasm (Lesson 4).

dw.Amlodipine: A CCB: safe in asthma.
dw.Hydrochlorothiazide: A thiazide: safe in asthma.

bank.q: Name the MOST potent loop diuretic (the smallest dose).
bank.why: Bumetanide 0.5–2 mg; furosemide 20–80 mg; ethacrynic acid is the least potent.

bank.q: Give the brand name of furosemide, the most commonly used loop diuretic.
bank.why: Furosemide = Lasix.

bank.q: Loop diuretics block which transporter in the thick ascending limb?
bank.why: NKCC2 = the Na+/K+/2Cl− cotransporter.

bank.q: Thiazides block which transporter in the distal convoluted tubule?
bank.why: NCC = the Na+/Cl− cotransporter.

bank.q: Name the prototype thiazide diuretic.
bank.why: HCTZ, 25–100 mg once a day.

bank.q: Loop diuretics are used first and foremost for which emergency?
bank.why: Uses: acute pulmonary edema, hyperkalemia, acute renal failure.

bank.q: Julianne hears ringing in the ears after IV diuretics for heart failure. Which diuretic CLASS causes this?
bank.why: Loop diuretics are ototoxic (the ear has a loop too).

bank.q: Janah has gout two months after starting a diuretic for hypertension. Which diuretic CLASS?
bank.why: Thiazide toxicity = LUNA: lipids up, uric acid up (gout), Na+ down, allergy.

bank.q: Which electrolyte problem do potassium-sparing diuretics cause?
bank.why: They spare K+, so K+ builds up.

bank.q: Which potassium-sparing diuretic causes gynecomastia?
bank.why: Spironolactone is a steroid look-alike; eplerenone is the more selective one.

bank.q: Which diuretic class acts at the collecting duct?
bank.why: A-O-L-T-K down the nephron: the K-sparing diuretics act last, at the collecting duct.

bank.q: Which drug CLASS lowers angiotensin II and raises bradykinin?
bank.why: ACE inhibitors (-pril) block ACE = kininase II.

bank.q: Tracy's dry cough on captopril comes from the build-up of which substance?
bank.why: ACE also breaks down bradykinin; blocking it raises bradykinin → cough, angioedema.

bank.q: ACE is the same enzyme as which kininase?
bank.why: ACE = kininase II, which inactivates bradykinin.

bank.q: A patient's ACE-inhibitor cough is managed by switching to which drug CLASS?
bank.why: ARBs block the AT1 receptor and leave bradykinin alone: no cough.

bank.q: ARBs block which angiotensin II receptor subtype?
bank.why: AT1 effects (vasoconstriction, aldosterone…) are blocked; AT2 is left alone.

bank.q: Name the drug that blocks renin.
bank.why: Aliskiren = the direct renin inhibitor (-kiren).

bank.q: Which organ releases renin?
bank.why: Kidney renin → angiotensinogen (liver) → Ang I → ACE (lungs) → Ang II.

bank.q: Where does most ACE come from?
bank.why: ACE (from the lungs) turns angiotensin I into angiotensin II.

bank.q: Angiotensin II makes the adrenal gland release which hormone?
bank.why: Aldosterone → the kidneys reabsorb salt and water → more volume, higher BP.

bank.q: Name the central α2 agonist used for hypertension in pregnancy.
bank.why: Methyldopa = Mom's drug.

bank.term: K+ channel opener with hair growth
bank.q: Name the oral vasodilator that opens K+ channels and causes hair growth.
bank.why: Minoxidil and diazoxide open K+ channels; topical minoxidil 5% is a hair-regrowth product.

bank.q: Name the IV vasodilator that activates dopamine receptors.
bank.why: Fenol-DOPA-m.

bank.q: Name the most commonly used calcium channel blocker.
bank.why: Lecture: amlodipine is the most common CCB.

bank.q: Verapamil is one non-dihydropyridine CCB. Name the other.
bank.why: Verapamil and diltiazem also slow the SA node.

bank.q: Hypertension with no identifiable cause is called ___ hypertension.
bank.why: Primary (essential) = no specific cause; secondary = has a specific etiology.

bank.q: BP still uncontrolled on 3 drugs, one of them a diuretic, is called ___ hypertension.
bank.why: Resistant hypertension → refer to a specialist.

bank.q: A low-risk patient tries lifestyle changes for how many months before drugs are started?
bank.why: Not high risk → lifestyle for 3 months; target not reached → start drugs.

bank.q: Inflammation is best described as the immune system's...
bank.a: Protective response to an injurious stimulus
d: Permanent destruction of tissue after infection
bank.why: Inflammation is the immune system's protective response to an injurious stimulus. Dr. Orig: be thankful for it, because it protects the body.

dw.Failure to recognize an injury: It is a working, protective response, not a failure.
dw.Permanent destruction of tissue after in: It is meant to resolve; it is not permanent damage.
dw.Reaction seen only in allergy: Allergy is one trigger; injury and infection cause it too.

bank.q: Which can evoke inflammation?
bank.a: Noxious agents, infections and physical injuries
d: Bacterial and viral infections of the skin
Physical injuries such as cuts and wounds
Allergens such as pollen and dust
bank.why: Inflammation can be evoked by noxious agents (poisons), infections and physical injuries.

dw.Bacterial and viral infections of the sk: Poisons and physical injuries also cause it.
dw.Physical injuries such as cuts and wound: Infections and noxious agents also cause it.
dw.Allergens such as pollen and dust: Allergens are only one possible trigger.

bank.q: Which Latin term means heat?
bank.why: Calor = heat (think calorie). The five cardinal signs: calor, rubor, tumor, dolor, functio laesa.

bank.q: The Latin term rubor refers to...
bank.why: Rubor = redness.

bank.q: In the five cardinal signs, tumor means...
bank.why: Tumor = swelling, here not a cancer.

dw.Loss of function: Loss of function is functio laesa.

bank.q: The Latin term dolor means...
bank.why: Dolor = pain.

dw.Loss of function: Loss of function is functio laesa.

bank.q: Functio laesa is the cardinal sign of...
bank.why: Functio laesa = loss of function: with heat, redness, swelling and pain you cannot use the part.

bank.q: Which is NOT one of the five cardinal signs of inflammation?
bank.why: The five are calor, rubor, tumor, dolor and functio laesa. Fever is a systemic response driven by PGE2 in the hypothalamus, not one of the five.

dw.Loss of function (functio laesa): Loss of function is a cardinal sign.

bank.q: Heat and redness of an inflamed area are due mainly to...
bank.a: Local vasodilation bringing more blood to the site
d: Fluid leaking out of the small vessels
Activated nociceptors in the skin and tissue
Loss of function of the injured tissue
bank.why: Vasodilation sends all the blood to the injury, so it is warm (calor) and red (rubor).

dw.Loss of function of the injured tissue: That is a result, not the cause of heat and redness.

bank.q: Swelling in inflammation is due mainly to...
bank.a: Increased capillary permeability, so fluid and cells leave the vessel
d: Vasoconstriction that traps blood inside the small vessels
Activation of nociceptors by heat, acid or pressure
A drop in local blood flow to the injured tissue
bank.why: The gaps between endothelial cells widen so white blood cells can leave; blood fluid goes out with them and the tissue swells (tumor).

dw.A drop in local blood flow to the injure: Blood flow rises at the injury.

bank.q: Pain in inflammation arises because...
bank.a: Nociceptors are activated and made more sensitive
d: Blood vessels constrict around the nerves of the area
Leukocytes die and block the nerve fibers of the area
The hypothalamic set point rises, warming the area
bank.why: Prostaglandins increase the sensitivity of nociceptors, so even a light touch hurts.

dw.Leukocytes die and block the nerve fiber: Dead leukocytes form pus; they do not cause the pain.

bank.q: Which describes inflammation?
bank.a: Transient local vasodilation and increased capillary permeability
d: Local vasoconstriction with reduced capillary permeability
bank.why: Inflammation: transient local vasodilation + increased capillary permeability, infiltration of leukocytes and phagocytes, then resolution.

dw.Local vasoconstriction with reduced capi: It is the opposite: dilation and increased permeability.
dw.Permanent fibrosis in every case: Resolution can occur with or without fibrosis.

bank.q: Why does the body increase capillary permeability at an injury?
bank.a: So white blood cells can leave the vessel and reach the injury
d: So the vessel can store more blood for later use
So platelets can stop the bleeding from the vessel
So nociceptors can be blocked and the pain relieved
bank.why: The WBCs fight off infection; they must leave the vessel to reach it.

dw.So the vessel can store more blood for l: The purpose is to let cells out, not store blood.
dw.So nociceptors can be blocked and the pa: Nothing blocks nociceptors here; they are activated.

bank.q: At the site of injury, the infiltrating white blood cells will...
bank.a: Phagocytize bacteria to help clear the infection
d: Block prostaglandin synthesis at the site of injury
Raise the pain threshold of the nerves nearby
Lower the body temperature at the injured site
bank.why: The infiltrating leukocytes and phagocytic cells eat the bacteria.

dw.Raise the pain threshold of the nerves n: That is the action of an analgesic such as paracetamol.
dw.Lower the body temperature at the injure: They help raise it through pyrogens.

bank.q: In which patients may inflammation fail to resolve, leaving a chronically inflamed area?
d: Healthy young adults with a clean wound
Patients with only a short fever
Patients whose wounds heal within a few days
bank.why: In diabetics the body cannot return to homeostasis, so the inflammation lasts years (diabetic foot) until ulcers and amputation.

dw.Healthy young adults with a clean wound: Their inflammation usually resolves in days.
dw.Patients with only a short fever: A short fever is a normal, resolving response.
dw.Patients whose wounds heal within a few: Healing in days means resolution did occur.

bank.q: A diabetic patient's foot is red, swollen and painful. Which Latin terms match these three signs, in that order?
bank.why: Red = rubor, swollen = tumor, painful = dolor.

dw.Calor, rubor, tumor: That has heat, which wasn't described, and misses pain.
dw.Tumor, calor, functio laesa: That doesn't match red, swollen, painful in order.
dw.Dolor, calor, rubor: The order is wrong: red, swollen, painful = rubor, tumor, dolor.

bank.q: Which are the primary prostanoids that mediate inflammation?
bank.why: PGE2 and PGI2 increase local blood flow, vascular permeability and leukocyte infiltration.

dw.PGD2 and leukotriene B4: PGD2 has a minor allergic role; leukotrienes are not prostanoids.
dw.Thromboxane A2 and PGD2: TXA2 is prothrombotic and from COX-1; PGD2 is minor.
dw.Histamine and bradykinin: These are mediators but not prostanoids.

bank.q: What do PGE2 and PGI2 do in inflammation?
bank.a: Raise blood flow, permeability and WBC infiltration
d: Decrease blood flow and capillary permeability
Block nociceptors to reduce the pain of the area
Lower the hypothalamic set point to cool the body down
bank.why: They are the vasodilating, leaky-vessel prostaglandins.

dw.Decrease blood flow and capillary permea: They cause vasodilation and more permeability.

bank.q: Which prostanoid has a minor role in allergic responses?
bank.why: PGD2 has a minor allergic effect; prostaglandins are mostly about inflammation, leukotrienes about allergy.

dw.PGE2: PGE2 is a primary inflammatory prostanoid.
dw.PGI2: PGI2 is a primary inflammatory prostanoid.

bank.q: Arachidonic acid is released from membrane phospholipids by the enzyme...
bank.why: Lipase breaks down lipids: phospholipase A2 frees arachidonic acid from the membrane.

dw.Cyclooxygenase: COX converts arachidonic acid after it is released.
dw.Lipoxygenase: LOX converts arachidonic acid after it is released.

bank.q: Arachidonic acid is a type of...
bank.why: Arachidonic acid is a fatty acid found in membrane phospholipids.

dw.Steroid hormone: It is a fatty acid, not a steroid.

bank.q: Once freed, arachidonic acid can follow which two pathways?
bank.a: The COX pathway and the LOX pathway
d: The COX pathway and the ACE pathway
The LOX pathway and the CYP pathway
The renin pathway and the COX pathway
bank.why: COX (cyclooxygenase) makes prostaglandins; LOX (lipoxygenase) makes leukotrienes.

bank.q: The cyclooxygenase pathway forms...
bank.why: COX forms prostaglandins (and thromboxane).

dw.Histamine: Histamine comes from mast cells, not COX.
dw.Cytokines: Cytokines are not made by COX.

bank.q: The lipoxygenase pathway forms...
bank.why: LOX forms leukotrienes, linked to allergy and asthma.

dw.Bradykinin: Bradykinin is not made from arachidonic acid.

bank.q: Montelukast, taken for asthma and allergic rhinitis, blocks...
bank.why: Montelukast is a leukotriene blocker. Leukotrienes are about allergy; prostaglandins are about inflammation.

dw.Histamine at H1 receptors: That is what antihistamines such as chlorphenamine do.

bank.q: Which statement is correct?
bank.a: Prostaglandins: mostly inflammation; leukotrienes: mostly allergy
d: Leukotrienes: mostly inflammation; prostaglandins: mostly allergy
Both are mainly about allergy and asthma
Both are made by the cyclooxygenase pathway
bank.why: COX → prostaglandins (inflammation, pain, fever); LOX → leukotrienes (allergy).

bank.q: Prostaglandins cause pain in inflammation by...
bank.why: Prostaglandins make nociceptors more sensitive, so a touch is enough to hurt.

bank.q: Nociceptors are...
d: White blood cells that sense injury
Receptors in the hypothalamus that sense temperature
bank.why: Noci means pain: nociceptors sense pain from heat, acid or pressure.

dw.White blood cells that sense injury: They are nerve fibers, not WBCs.

bank.q: Which brain structure regulates the set point of body temperature?
bank.why: The hypothalamus keeps the set point (about 37 °C); in fever the set point is raised.

dw.Medulla: The medulla handles breathing and heart rate.
dw.Cerebellum: The cerebellum handles balance and coordination.

bank.q: Which are pyrogens that raise the temperature set point?
bank.why: Pyrogens: IL-1, IL-6 and TNF-alpha. They act on the hypothalamus, which then makes PGE2.

dw.PGE2, PGI2 and PGD2: These are prostanoids; PGE2 acts after the pyrogens.
dw.Histamine, bradykinin and serotonin: These are not the fever pyrogens.

bank.q: The pyrogens make the hypothalamus secrete which prostanoid to raise the set point?
bank.why: IL-1, IL-6 and TNF-alpha → hypothalamus → PGE2 → higher set point → fever. Prostaglandins again.

dw.PGD2: PGD2 has a minor allergic role.
dw.PGI2: PGI2 is a vasodilator in inflammation.

bank.q: Why does the body raise its temperature set point during infection?
bank.a: To speed blood flow and white blood cell recruitment
d: To slow the heart rate and save energy
To stop prostaglandin synthesis in the tissue
To block the pyrogens in the blood
bank.why: A higher temperature helps the response: faster blood flow and WBC recruitment.

dw.To stop prostaglandin synthesis in the t: Fever uses PGE2; it doesn't stop it.

bank.q: Kyle has a low-grade fever from a cold. She is resting at home and is comfortable. What is the best approach?
bank.a: Let the fever run its course
d: Give ibuprofen right away to bring it to normal
bank.why: Dr. Orig: if you can tolerate it, leave the fever alone, because it is your body's response to infection. Treat it when it is uncomfortable or deleterious.

dw.Give ibuprofen right away to bring it to: A tolerable fever is a useful response; treat it only if uncomfortable.
dw.Give paracetamol every 4 hours: It isn't needed for a tolerable fever.
dw.Start aspirin: It isn't needed, and aspirin has GI risks.

bank.q: A 65-year-old with pneumonia has a normal temperature. Which explanation fits?
bank.a: Elderly or immunocompromised patients may not fever
d: Pneumonia never causes any fever in anyone
NSAIDs permanently lower the temperature set point
The hypothalamus plays no part in a fever
bank.why: Dr. Orig: patients with a poor inflammatory response (elderly, immunocompromised) may not fever even with pneumonia.

bank.q: NSAID stands for...
bank.why: NSAIDs are anti-inflammatory drugs that are not steroids.

bank.q: Why are they called non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs?
bank.a: Steroids also reduce inflammation; these are not steroids
d: They contain no salicylates at all in the tablet or capsule
They do not act on prostaglandins at any step of the pathway
They are food supplements and not true drugs at all
bank.why: Steroid creams and other steroids are anti-inflammatory too; NSAIDs are the non-steroidal group.

dw.They contain no salicylates at all in th: Aspirin is a salicylate and an NSAID.

bank.q: NSAIDs are classified as...
bank.a: Non-selective NSAIDs and COX-2 selective NSAIDs
d: COX-1 selective and LOX selective NSAIDs
bank.why: Non-selective (both COX-1 and COX-2) vs COX-2 selective (coxibs).

dw.COX-1 selective and LOX selective NSAIDs: The two groups are non-selective and COX-2 selective.

bank.q: What is the mechanism of action common to all NSAIDs?
bank.why: All NSAIDs are COX inhibitors, so there is no separate mechanism to memorize.

dw.Inhibition of phospholipase A2: That enzyme is upstream of COX; NSAIDs act on COX.

bank.q: The principal effects of NSAIDs are due to...
bank.why: Inhibiting COX lowers prostaglandins: less inflammation, pain and fever.

dw.Blocking nociceptors directly: They reduce the prostaglandins that sensitize them.

bank.q: COX-1 is...
d: The enzyme of the LOX pathway
bank.why: COX-1 is constitutive (always there) and does housekeeping: stomach lining, renal blood flow, platelets.

bank.q: COX-2 is the...
bank.a: Inducible COX making the prostaglandins of inflammation
d: Enzyme of the LOX pathway that makes leukotrienes
Receptor for PGE2 on the endothelium
bank.why: COX-2 is induced by inflammation; it is the source of prostanoids for inflammation and cancer.

bank.q: Which is a housekeeping function of COX-1 prostaglandins?
bank.a: Blood flow to the stomach lining and kidneys
d: Producing fever by acting on the hypothalamus
Swelling at wound sites during inflammation
Making leukotrienes for asthma and rhinitis
bank.why: COX-1 prostaglandins keep vessels open to the GI tract and kidney; that is why blocking them causes ulcers and renal problems.

bank.q: COX-2 selective NSAIDs were made to...
bank.a: Reduce GI adverse effects by sparing COX-1
d: Block leukotrienes in the airways and nasal passages
Raise the pain threshold only, like paracetamol
Inhibit COX-1 more strongly than COX-2 does
bank.why: Selective COX-2 inhibition reduces GI complications.

bank.q: Which are the three therapeutic uses of NSAIDs?
bank.why: Therapeutic uses: inflammation, pain and fever.

dw.Infection, allergy and asthma: NSAIDs are not antibiotics or anti-allergy drugs.
dw.Pain, infection and cough: They don't treat infection or cough.
dw.Inflammation, hypertension and seizures: They may raise BP, and aren't antiseizure drugs.

bank.q: NSAIDs give symptomatic relief in which group of disorders?
bank.why: NSAIDs relieve pain from musculoskeletal disorders such as RA, osteoarthritis and gout; they all have inflammation.

bank.q: NSAIDs are effective against pain that is...
bank.a: Of low to moderate intensity, mostly inflammatory
d: Severe, as in metastatic cancer of the bone
Only neuropathic pain from nerve injury
Only visceral pain from the abdominal organs
bank.why: NSAIDs: low-to-moderate inflammatory pain. Severe or breakthrough pain (stage 4 cancer) needs opioids.

dw.Only visceral pain from the abdominal or: That is not a limit taught.

bank.q: A patient with stage 4 cancer spread to the bone has pain of 10 out of 10. Which drug is appropriate?
bank.why: Severe pain needs an opioid such as morphine. NSAIDs and paracetamol cover low-to-moderate pain.

dw.Ibuprofen: An NSAID cannot control pain this severe.
dw.Celecoxib: A coxib is not stronger for pain.
dw.Paracetamol: It is only for low-to-moderate pain.

bank.q: A patient with appendicitis has pain that paracetamol or ibuprofen can cover. What is the better first choice?
bank.a: Either of those two, not morphine
d: Morphine right away for the pain
bank.why: Dr. Orig: for low-to-moderate pain use an NSAID or paracetamol; opioids carry the risk of addiction.

dw.Morphine right away for the pain: Morphine can cause addiction and is for severe pain.
dw.Montelukast, the leukotriene blocker: It is a leukotriene blocker for allergy.
dw.Amlodipine, the calcium channel blocker: It is a calcium channel blocker for hypertension.

bank.q: Eliza has primary dysmenorrhea. Which drug is first-line, ideally started before the flow begins?
bank.why: First-line for primary dysmenorrhea is an NSAID, taken prophylactically before the pain starts.

dw.Montelukast: A leukotriene blocker for asthma and allergic rhinitis.
dw.Amlodipine: A calcium channel blocker for hypertension.

bank.q: Which can be tried for a migraine attack that rest and hydration alone cannot control?
bank.why: NSAIDs can be used for migraine attacks.

dw.Montelukast: It is for allergy and asthma.

bank.q: NSAIDs are reserved for fever that is...
bank.a: Deleterious, as in a high-grade fever
d: Of any degree, even if it is mild and tolerable
Seen only in infants and young children
Below 37.5 °C, even if the person feels well
bank.why: Treat fever only when it may be deleterious or you are uncomfortable; a high-grade fever (about 40 °C with rigors) is treated.

dw.Of any degree, even if it is mild and to: A tolerable fever can be left alone.
dw.Seen only in infants and young children: Fever management is not limited to infants.
dw.Below 37.5 °C, even if the person feels: That is not a fever needing treatment.

bank.q: Marielle has a temperature of 40 °C with chills. Which drug is appropriate?
bank.why: A fever this high is deleterious, so an antipyretic such as paracetamol is given.

dw.Montelukast: A leukotriene blocker for allergy and asthma.
dw.Morphine: An opioid for severe pain, not fever.
dw.Amlodipine: A calcium channel blocker for hypertension.

bank.q: A patient who drank heavily wakes up with a red, swollen, painful big toe. Uric acid is high. Which drug relieves the inflammation?
bank.why: Uric acid crystals in the joint attract WBCs, giving the five cardinal signs (gout). NSAIDs stop the inflammation.

dw.Morphine: An opioid does not treat inflammation.

bank.q: Which are the three groups of NSAID adverse effects?
d: Hepatic, pulmonary and ocular adverse effects
Neurologic, dermatologic and endocrine adverse effects
Hematologic, otologic and urinary adverse effects
bank.why: NSAID adverse effects: GI, cardiovascular, and blood pressure and renal.

dw.Hepatic, pulmonary and ocular adverse ef: These are not the groups taught.
dw.Neurologic, dermatologic and endocrine a: These are not the groups taught.
dw.Hematologic, otologic and urinary advers: These are not the groups taught.

bank.q: The most common adverse effects of NSAIDs are...
bank.a: Gastrointestinal, such as nausea, vomiting and abdominal pain
d: Hepatic failure with jaundice and rising liver enzymes
Hypotension with dizziness on standing up quickly
Ototoxicity with ringing in the ears and hearing loss
bank.why: GI symptoms are the most common NSAID problem.

dw.Hepatic failure with jaundice and rising: That is a paracetamol overdose problem.
dw.Ototoxicity with ringing in the ears and: That is a loop diuretic problem.

bank.q: Chronic NSAID use causes gastric ulcers because...
bank.a: Prostaglandin blood flow to the stomach lining falls
d: NSAIDs raise stomach acid by stimulating COX-2 there
NSAIDs kill the normal bacteria of the whole gut
NSAIDs block leukotrienes in the stomach wall
bank.why: COX-1 prostaglandins keep blood flowing to the GI lining; blocked, the lining is easily injured.

dw.NSAIDs raise stomach acid by stimulating: NSAIDs inhibit COX; the problem is lost protection.

bank.q: A serious GI complication of NSAIDs includes...
d: Hyperkalemia with a high potassium level
bank.why: Ulcers from NSAIDs may bleed, perforate or obstruct.

dw.Hyperkalemia with a high potassium level: That is a potassium-sparing diuretic or ACE inhibitor issue.

bank.q: A patient with osteoarthritis takes ibuprofen every day and now vomits blood. What most likely happened?
bank.a: An NSAID-induced gastric ulcer that bled
d: Acetaminophen hepatotoxicity from toxic NAPQI buildup
COX-2 thrombosis in a stomach vessel
bank.why: Chronic NSAID use removes the protective prostaglandins and causes ulcers that can bleed.

dw.Analgesic nephropathy from chronic use: That is slowly progressive renal failure.
dw.COX-2 thrombosis in a stomach vessel: That is a coxib problem causing clots.

bank.q: NSAIDs should NEVER be given to a patient with...
bank.why: If a patient has black or bloody stools or vomits blood, no NSAIDs: they worsen the bleeding.

dw.Fever: Fever may be treated if deleterious.

bank.q: A patient with a heart attack is about to get aspirin. Which question is most important to ask first?
bank.a: Is there blood in the stool, vomit or nose?
d: Does the patient have a fever above 38 °C today?
Does the patient drink coffee every morning?
Does the patient take vitamin C every morning?
bank.why: Dr. Orig's story: aspirin was loaded in a patient with a hidden GI bleed and the patient died. Always ask about GI bleeding before an NSAID.

dw.Does the patient have a fever above 38 °: Fever does not change aspirin use.

bank.q: Why do COX-2 selective NSAIDs carry a cardiovascular risk?
bank.a: They leave COX-1 thromboxane A2 intact, and it is prothrombotic
d: They block prostacyclin only and leave the platelets alone
They block COX-1 in platelets and thin the blood too much
They cause hypotension that leads to fainting and falls
bank.why: TXA2 is prothrombotic and atherogenic; coxibs don't inhibit it, so clots, heart attack and stroke are possible.

dw.They block prostacyclin only and leave t: The key issue is unopposed thromboxane A2.
dw.They block COX-1 in platelets and thin t: They spare COX-1, which is why TXA2 is still made.
dw.They cause hypotension that leads to fai: They are not known for hypotension.

bank.q: Thromboxane A2 is...
bank.why: TXA2 (from COX-1) increases clot formation.

bank.q: Which patient should NOT be given celecoxib?
bank.a: A patient who had a myocardial infarction
d: A patient with a past gastric ulcer and GERD
bank.why: Never give COX-2 selective inhibitors to patients with a history of MI or stroke.

dw.A patient with a past gastric ulcer and: Celecoxib is chosen for those with GI problems.
dw.A patient with primary dysmenorrhea: An NSAID is first-line, and a coxib is allowed.

bank.q: About what percent of NSAID users develop hypertension?
bank.why: About 5% of NSAID users develop hypertension.

bank.q: Analgesic nephropathy is...
bank.a: Slowly progressive renal failure from chronic NSAIDs
d: Acute liver failure after one very large dose of a drug
