Gastric ulceration caused by long NSAID use
Hypertension from sodium retention, nothing more
bank.why: Chronic NSAID users lose prostaglandin-driven renal blood flow and their kidneys fail slowly.

dw.Hypertension from sodium retention, noth: It is kidney failure, not only hypertension.

bank.q: Chronic NSAIDs harm the kidneys because...
bank.a: Prostaglandin-driven renal blood flow is lost
d: They directly dissolve the nephrons of the kidney
They raise renal prostaglandins and widen the vessels
They block renin release from the kidney only
bank.why: COX-1 prostaglandins keep blood flowing to the kidney.

dw.They directly dissolve the nephrons of t: The harm comes from reduced blood flow.

bank.q: Elijah has taken mefenamic acid daily for months. Now there is hypertension and creatinine is rising. Which adverse effects fit?
bank.a: NSAID action on blood pressure and kidney (analgesic nephropathy)
d: Acetaminophen hepatotoxicity with jaundice from NAPQI
A coxib-induced thrombosis with a clot in the leg
Salicylate poisoning with ringing in the ears and fast breathing
bank.why: Chronic NSAID use raises BP in about 5% and can cause analgesic nephropathy.

dw.A coxib-induced thrombosis with a clot i: Mefenamic acid is not a coxib.

bank.q: Aspirin belongs to which group?
bank.why: Aspirin is acetylsalicylic acid, a salicylate.

dw.Propionic acid derivatives: These are ibuprofen, naproxen and ketoprofen.
dw.Fenamates: These are mefenamic acid and relatives.

bank.q: Which drugs are salicylates?
d: Celecoxib, etoricoxib and the other coxibs
Mefenamic acid, flufenamic acid and meclofenamate
bank.why: Salicylates: aspirin, salicylic acid, methyl salicylate, sulfasalazine, mesalamine.

bank.q: Another name for aspirin is...
bank.why: Aspirin = acetylsalicylic acid.

dw.Salicylic acid: Salicylic acid is the skin exfoliant, not aspirin itself.

bank.q: Aspirin differs from the other NSAIDs because it...
bank.why: Aspirin is a strong, irreversible COX inhibitor.

bank.q: The usual oral aspirin dose as an analgesic-antipyretic is...
d: 50 to 150 mg in a single dose
bank.why: Aspirin 325-1,000 mg orally every 4-6 hours.

dw.50 to 150 mg in a single dose: That is a diclofenac range from the slide.

bank.q: Aspirin is used as an...
bank.why: Aspirin: analgesic (anti-pain) and antipyretic (anti-fever).

dw.Antihistamine and decongestant: That is for allergy and colds.
dw.Diuretic and antihypertensive: That is not an aspirin use.

bank.q: Which salicylate is used for inflammatory bowel disease?
bank.why: Mesalamine for inflammatory bowel disease; sulfasalazine for rheumatoid arthritis.

dw.Salicylic acid: That is used on the skin.
dw.Aspirin: Aspirin is not the IBD drug.

bank.q: Which salicylate is used for rheumatoid arthritis?
bank.why: Sulfasalazine is the salicylate for rheumatoid arthritis.

dw.Salicylic acid: That is used on the skin.

bank.q: Salicylic acid in skin care and wart plasters acts as...
bank.a: An exfoliant that peels the outer skin layer
d: A COX-2 selective inhibitor taken by mouth
An oral analgesic-antipyretic for pain and fever
An antihistamine used for allergic rhinitis
bank.why: Salicylic acid is used for warts, corns and fungal skin infections.

bank.q: Christopher has a wart. Which drug is infused in the plaster Christopher should use?
bank.why: Salicylic acid plasters peel off the layer of skin with the wart.

dw.Mefenamic acid: It is a fenamate taken by mouth.

bank.q: Which NSAID is loaded in a patient with a myocardial infarction?
bank.why: Aspirin is the standard drug for MI, but check for GI bleeding first.

dw.Ibuprofen: It is not the standard for MI.
dw.Ketorolac: It is for severe pain, not MI.

bank.q: Acetaminophen is also called...
bank.why: Acetaminophen = paracetamol (Tylenol, Biogesic).

dw.Ibuprofen: Ibuprofen is a propionic acid derivative.

bank.q: Compared with other NSAIDs, the anti-inflammatory effect of acetaminophen is...
d: Absent, because it does not inhibit COX
bank.why: Paracetamol works mostly on pain and fever and has only a weak anti-inflammatory effect.

dw.Absent, because it does not inhibit COX: It is a non-selective COX inhibitor.

bank.q: What is the mechanism of acetaminophen?
bank.a: A non-selective COX inhibitor, weakly anti-inflammatory
d: A selective COX-2 inhibitor that spares the stomach
An irreversible COX inhibitor of the platelets
A leukotriene receptor blocker for the airways
bank.why: It raises the threshold to painful stimuli (analgesic) and lowers fever.

bank.q: Acetaminophen is mainly used for...
bank.why: Mainly an analgesic and antipyretic.

bank.q: Acetaminophen is...
bank.why: It can also be combined with other analgesics, opioid and non-opioid.

bank.q: The typical acetaminophen dose is...
bank.why: Typical dose 325-650 mg every 4-6 hours.

dw.1 to 2 g every 4 to 6 hours: That would quickly pass the daily limit.

bank.q: For an adult, the total daily dose of acetaminophen should not exceed...
bank.why: Maximum 4 g a day (2 g for chronic alcoholics).

dw.1 g: That is below the usual limit.
dw.2 g: That is the limit for chronic alcoholics.

bank.q: For a chronic alcoholic, the daily limit of acetaminophen is...
bank.why: The liver of a chronic alcoholic is at higher risk, so the limit is 2 g.

bank.q: Frances takes 500 mg paracetamol tablets. What is the most she should take in a day?
bank.why: 8 x 500 mg = 4 g, the daily maximum.

bank.q: Which toxic metabolite causes the liver injury in acetaminophen overdose?
bank.why: NAPQI causes hepatocyte necrosis, leading to liver failure.

bank.q: Hepatotoxicity may follow a single acetaminophen dose of about...
bank.why: A single dose of 10-15 g can cause hepatotoxicity.

dw.1 to 2 g: That is within the daily limit.
dw.3 to 4 g: That is within the daily limit.
dw.100 g: That is far above the toxic dose.

bank.q: A potentially fatal acetaminophen dose is about...
bank.a: 20 to 25 g or more in one dose
d: 5 to 10 g in a single dose
10 to 15 g in a single dose
2 to 4 g in a single dose
bank.why: 20-25 g or more can be fatal (about 40 tablets of 500 mg).

dw.5 to 10 g in a single dose: That is below the fatal range.
dw.10 to 15 g in a single dose: That causes hepatotoxicity but is not the fatal range.
dw.2 to 4 g in a single dose: That is a normal daily dose.

bank.q: Janah takes Neozep, Bioflu and Biogesic within a few hours for flu symptoms. What is the main danger?
bank.a: Too much paracetamol, since all three have it
d: Too much phenylephrine alone from all three of them
An allergic reaction to the caffeine in them
bank.why: Neozep, Bioflu and Biogesic all contain paracetamol; added together they can pass 4 g a day.

dw.Too much phenylephrine alone from all th: The shared drug in all three is paracetamol.
dw.An allergic reaction to the caffeine in: None of the three contains caffeine.
dw.Aspirin-induced bleeding from the three: None of the three contains aspirin.

bank.q: Which brands all contain paracetamol?
bank.why: Each cold or pain remedy listed also contains paracetamol, so they cannot be stacked.

bank.q: Neozep is paracetamol plus...
bank.why: Neozep = phenylephrine + paracetamol.

dw.Caffeine: That is in Rexidol and Saridon.

bank.q: Which antihistamine is in Bioflu?

notes: Safety numbers

Therapeutic index — TD50 ÷ ED50 (higher = safer); slide: 6 ÷ 2 = 3 | Margin of safety — LD1 ÷ ED99 (uses the extremes) | Memory tip — TI uses the middles (50s), margin of safety the edges (1 and 99); bad number on top
4 types of drug toxicity (DAID)

Dose-dependent — worse with concentration and duration | Allergic — hypersensitivity types I–IV | Idiosyncratic — peculiar to one person; primaquine → hemolytic anemia in 10% of black males | Drug-drug interactions — absorption, protein binding, metabolism, receptor, therapeutic action
Dose-dependent examples

Barbiturates — CNS depression (dose-dependent) | Antipsychotics — tardive dyskinesia (duration-dependent) | Tetracyclines — phototoxicity | Acetaminophen — NAPQI → hepatic necrosis (pathological) | Radiation, chemicals, chemo — genotoxic → mutagenic, carcinogenic | Mnemonic — BARBS = brain down (dose); TARDIVE = tardy (time); TETRAcycline + sun = phototoxic; NAPQI = the Nasty Acetaminophen Product
Extrapyramidal symptoms (D-P-A-T)

Acute dystonia — hours to 5 days; tongue, neck, face spasm | Parkinsonism — 5–30 days; tremor, shuffling gait | Akathisia — 5–60 days; restlessness | Tardive dyskinesia — months to years; lip-smacking, fly-catching tongue
Hypersensitivity (ACID)
Type I — Anaphylactic: IgE, mast cells, histamine | Type II — Cytolytic (cytotoxic) | Type III — Arthus reaction (immune complex) | Type IV — Delayed (T cells)
Drug-drug interactions

Absorption — ranitidine raises GI pH → more triazolam absorbed | Protein binding — aspirin, barbiturates, phenytoin, sulfonamides, valproic acid, warfarin get displaced | Metabolism — ethanol induces CYP2E1 | Receptor — buprenorphine (partial agonist) blocks narcotic euphoria | Therapeutic action — additive, synergistic, antagonistic | Mnemonic — Follow the drug's journey: Absorbed → rides Proteins → Metabolized → hits a Receptor → Therapeutic action ("Ang Pasyente May Reseta Today")
4 kinds of antagonism (F-C-D-R)

Functional — opposite effects via different receptors | Chemical — binds the drug (EDTA chelates Ca and lead) | Dispositional — changes its ADME | Receptor — competitive (surmountable) or noncompetitive
Treating poisoning

Priorities — vital functions; less absorption, more elimination; fight the effects | ABCDE — airway, breathing, circulation, disability (O2, dextrose, naloxone, thiamine), exposure | First step of decontamination — stop the exposure; wash eyes and skin | GI decontamination needs — dangerous poison, still unabsorbed, can be done safely | GI methods — activated charcoal, whole-bowel irrigation, cathartics, gastric lavage, ipecac | Mnemonic — ABCDE first; the coma cocktail is "DONT": Dextrose, Oxygen, Naloxone, Thiamine (thiamine goes with the dextrose)
Antidotes: metals and alcohols

Dimercaprol (BAL), succimer (DMSA) — lead, mercury, arsenic | EDTA — lead | Penicillamine — lead, mercury, copper | Deferoxamine — iron (de-FE-roxamine) | Fomepizole, ethanol — methanol, ethylene glycol | Mnemonic — De-FE-roxamine = iron (Fe); PENNY-cillamine = copper (pennies are copper); BAL and succimer take the big three (lead, mercury, arsenic); Fomepizole = FOr the toxic alcohols
Antidotes: reverse the drug

Naloxone — opioids | Flumazenil — benzodiazepines | Atropine + pralidoxime (2-PAM) — organophosphates | Physostigmine — anticholinergic syndrome | Glucagon — β-blockers | High-dose insulin, calcium — calcium channel blockers | Digoxin immune Fab — digoxin | Sodium bicarbonate — Na channel blockers | Mnemonic — NaloxONE knocks out Narcotics; fluma-ZENIL → benZos; Atropine + Pralidoxime = "AP" for Agri-Pesticides; PHYSostigmine gets PHYSically into the brain; GLUCAgon gets around blocked β; DIGI-Fab for digoxin
Antidotes: blood and specific drugs

COX-1 — constitutive; housekeeping: GI mucosal protection, renal blood flow, platelet aggregation | COX-2 — inducible; prostanoids for inflammation and cancer | Non-selective NSAIDs — block both | COX-2 selective (coxibs) — spare COX-1; kinder to the GI tract | Mnemonic — COX-1 = ONE is always on (housekeeping: stomach and kidney); COX-2 = TWO shows up when called (inducible by inflammation)
NSAID uses

Inflammation — RA, osteoarthritis, gout (symptomatic relief) | Pain — low-to-moderate inflammatory pain; primary dysmenorrhea (first line, start before the flow); migraine | Fever — only if deleterious or uncomfortable | Severe pain (stage 4 cancer) — opioids, not NSAIDs
NSAID adverse effects

GI — most common (nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain); ulcer, bleeding, perforation, obstruction; ask about GI bleeding first | CV — coxibs leave TXA2 unopposed: MI, stroke | BP — about 5% develop hypertension | Renal — analgesic nephropathy (slowly progressive renal failure) | Mnemonic — GI, CV, BP, Renal: the Gut bleeds, Clots form (coxibs), Blood pressure rises, Renal flow falls
Salicylates and aspirin

Salicylates — aspirin, salicylic acid, methyl salicylate, sulfasalazine, mesalamine | Aspirin — acetylsalicylic acid; irreversible COX inhibitor; analgesic-antipyretic 325–1,000 mg every 4–6 h | Mesalamine — IBD | Sulfasalazine — RA | Salicylic acid — exfoliant for warts, corns and skin care | Aspirin is loaded in MI (check for bleeding first) | Mnemonic — SAL-icylates: aspirin, SAL-icylic acid, methyl SAL-icylate, sulfaSAL-azine, meSAL-amine; ASPIRIN = Always Stops Prostaglandins Irreversibly
Acetaminophen (paracetamol)

Raises the pain threshold; antipyretic; only weak anti-inflammatory; non-selective COX inhibitor | OTC; 325–650 mg every 4–6 h; max 4 g a day (2 g in chronic alcoholics) | NAPQI — toxic metabolite → hepatocyte necrosis | Single 10–15 g hepatotoxic; 20–25 g potentially fatal | Neozep (+ phenylephrine), Bioflu (+ phenylephrine + chlorphenamine), Tuseran (+ dextromethorphan + phenylpropanolamine), Rexidol and Saridon (+ caffeine), Skelan (+ naproxen) | Do not stack them | Mnemonic — PAIN and fever, little inflammation; 4 g = 8 tablets of 500 mg; NAPQI = the Nasty Acetaminophen Product; Neozep, Bioflu, Tuseran, Rexidol, Saridon and Skelan ALL carry paracetamol
Other NSAIDs

Diclofenac — potent; arthritis, dysmenorrhea, migraine; also a gel | Ketorolac — potent analgesic, moderate anti-inflammatory; oral, IV, IM; surgeons | Propionic acids — ibuprofen (Advil, Medicol), naproxen (Flanax, Skelan), ketoprofen; ibuprofen OTC at 200 mg or less, usual 400 mg every 4–6 h | Fenamates — mefenamic acid (Ponstan, Dolfenal); no advantage over other NSAIDs | Mnemonic — The "pro" drugs: ibuPROfen (Advil, Medicol), naPROxen (Flanax, Skelan), ketoPROfen; MEFenamic = Ponstan, Dolfenal; ketoROLAC = the surgeon's IV
COX-2 selective inhibitors

Celecoxib, etoricoxib | Chosen for patients with GI problems | Avoid in patients prone to cardiovascular or cerebrovascular disease (history of MI or stroke) | Not stronger painkillers | Rofecoxib was withdrawn for MI and stroke (slide only) | Mnemonic — coxIBs: cele-COXIB, etori-COXIB — kind to the stomach, careful with the heart (never after MI or stroke)
